translation_en:
Book of Documents

“Ah! You, Xi and He: the annual cycle comprises three hundred and sixty-six days. Use intercalary months to determine the four seasons and complete the year. Duly regulate the hundred offices, and all undertakings will flourish.”

Jiang Zhi

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Assistant Instructor: “Reconcile the intervals at which heaven, the sun, and the moon come together to establish intercalation. Only then does the annual cycle stand as an annual cycle, the year as a year, and the new moon become clear [?]. There are many principles involved here. Candidates in the examination hall generally fail to grasp the essentials, so their statements are confused and disordered, further obscuring the principles. This essay alone grasps them. It should be copied out to instruct the candidates.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: “Calendrical numbers are difficult to reconcile and also difficult to explain. This essay clearly explains the solar terms and new moons. Its author is evidently someone who does not speak lightly.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor: “The essay’s meaning is precise and appropriate, without a single empty phrase. It merits serving as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: “By adapting the commentary’s wording into an essay, the author achieves a natural, refined, and exact expression.”

The sage ruler issued a comprehensive charge to the calendrical officials, holding them responsible for successfully ordering the calendar and expecting thereby effective administration of the offices. How profoundly Heaven and humanity depend upon one another! If calendrical techniques do not depart from Heaven, government will not miss the proper seasons. Who could say that, once the calendar is perfected, government might fail to be perfected?

We may imagine that Emperor Yao’s intention in antiquity was this: ordering the calendar is the first task of government, and inserting intercalary months completes the work of constructing the calendar. You, Xi and He—why do you not devote your hearts fully to it? Why is this so? The sun …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
行之繞於地也日惟一周天行之健於日也日
惟一度積天日之贏縮而復於一周之始適氣
運之更始而遂爲一歲之朞焉一朞之中因天
日之差爲三百六十五度而有奇故歲日之數
爲三百六十六日而有定然歲以該月月以該
日則止於三百六十而歲運常舒月朔不足率
餘夫十日有奇故必合所餘之日而置閏積三
歲之餘而爲月使歲氣之有餘者有閏以消其
盈月朔之不足者有閏以益其虛則春夏秋冬
===
之序物候舉不忒其常而時令以正也子丑寅
卯以下辰位皆不易其次而歲功以成也斯可
謂全曆矣由是以之而授人也則令無爽忒而
率作於庶官者有常規政無僭違而責成於百
職者有定守將見政績之統於有位者自農桑
以降非一事也課功覈實之有所程皆及時而
惠叙矣治功之遊於在官者凡民事所關非一
端也月要歲會之有其度皆順時而叙次矣功
豈有不覆治豈有不成哉吁治道因於時而非
punctuated: 行之繞於地也，日惟一周；天行之健於日也，日惟一度。積天日之贏縮，而復於一周之始，適氣運之更始，而遂爲一歲之朞焉。一朞之中，因天日之差，爲三百六十五度而有奇，故歲日之數爲三百六十六日而有定。然歲以該月，月以該日，則止於三百六十，而歲運常舒，月朔不足，率餘夫十日有奇。故必合所餘之日而置閏，積三歲之餘而爲月，使歲氣之有餘者有閏以消其盈，月朔之不足者有閏以益其虛，則春夏秋冬之序，物候舉不忒其常，而時令以正也；子丑寅卯以下辰位，皆不易其次，而歲功以成也。斯可謂全曆矣！由是以之而授人也，則令無爽忒，而率作於庶官者有常規；政無僭違，而責成於百職者有定守。將見政績之統於有位者，自農桑以降，非一事也，課功覈實之有所程，皆及時而惠叙矣；治功之遊於在官者，凡民事所關，非一端也，月要歲會之有其度，皆順時而叙次矣。功豈有不覆，治豈有不成哉？吁！治道因於時，而非
translation_en:
…the sun’s movement around the earth completes one circuit each day; the movement of Heaven outpaces the sun by one degree each day. As the gains and losses between Heaven and the sun accumulate, they return to the starting point of a complete circuit, coinciding with the renewal of the cycle of seasonal qi and thus completing a year. Within this cycle, the difference between Heaven and the sun amounts to three hundred and sixty-five degrees and a fraction; hence the number of days in a year is fixed at three hundred and sixty-six. Yet if a year is reckoned by its months, and its months by their days, the total reaches only three hundred and sixty. The annual cycle regularly extends beyond this, while the lunar months fall short, leaving a surplus of somewhat more than ten days. It is therefore necessary to combine these surplus days and insert an intercalary month, accumulating the surplus of three years to make one month. Intercalation thus absorbs the excess in the annual cycle of seasonal qi and supplements the deficiency in the lunar months. Then, throughout the succession of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, the seasonal signs of living things never depart from their regular patterns, and the seasonal ordinances are properly aligned. The positions marked by the earthly branches, beginning with zi, chou, yin, and mao, likewise retain their proper sequence, and the work of the year is accomplished. This may indeed be called a complete calendar!
When this is used to communicate the proper seasons to the people, commands contain no errors, and there are regular rules for directing the work of the various officials. Government involves no overstepping or deviation, and there are fixed duties by which to hold the hundred offices accountable for results. One will then see that the achievements of government overseen by those in office encompass many tasks, beginning with agriculture and sericulture. With standards for assessing accomplishments and verifying actual results, all are attended to at the proper time and duly ordered. The accomplishments of administration that circulate among [?] serving officials concern the people’s affairs in many respects. With established measures for monthly summaries and annual accounts, all follow the seasons and are arranged in due sequence. How could accomplishments fail to be reviewed [?], or good government fail to be achieved? Ah! The way of government depends upon the seasons, and without…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
曆不明人時叙於曆而非閏不備聖人立法如
此其敬天勤民之意至矣抑考之叙堯典者首
以授時叙舜典者首以齊政蓋王者履端於始
故審時爲先歸餘於終故置閏爲備亦可見當
時君臣莫非通達天人貫徹三才者也後世俗
儒無事於曆而治曆者非儒何望其能明哉自
夏氏以來而羲和合爲一後世殆無專官矣何
望其能明哉
寬而有制從容以和
周宗正
===
同考試官訓導吳　批〔聖人所謂寬和者寬中自有制和中自有從容作者多以有制濟寬從容濟和殆失之矣此作得之宜録出以爲經學式〕
同考試官訓導張　批〔成王命君陳繼周公謹毖之後正欲其以寬和致治之意也此作發揮殆盡〕
考試官教授吳　批〔文字有筆力可取〕
考試官教授王　批〔讀是篇可以見忠厚立國意〕
思
punctuated:
曆不明，人時叙於曆而非閏不備。聖人立法如此，其敬天勤民之意至矣。抑考之，叙堯典者首以授時，叙舜典者首以齊政，蓋王者履端於始，故審時爲先；歸餘於終，故置閏爲備。亦可見當時君臣莫非通達天人、貫徹三才者也。後世俗儒無事於曆，而治曆者非儒，何望其能明哉？自夏氏以來，而羲和合爲一，後世殆無專官矣，何望其能明哉？
寬而有制，從容以和。
周宗正
同考試官訓導吳批〔聖人所謂寬和者，寬中自有制，和中自有從容。作者多以有制濟寬、從容濟和，殆失之矣。此作得之，宜録出以爲經學式。〕
同考試官訓導張批〔成王命君陳繼周公謹毖之後，正欲其以寬和致治之意也。此作發揮殆盡。〕
考試官教授吳批〔文字有筆力可取。〕
考試官教授王批〔讀是篇，可以見忠厚立國意。〕
思
translation_en:
…without a calendar, it cannot be understood. The seasons for human activities are ordered through the calendar, but without intercalary months that ordering is incomplete. Such were the laws established by the sages: their intention to revere Heaven and care diligently for the people was consummate. Moreover, examining the accounts, the Canon of Yao begins with granting the people the seasons, and the Canon of Shun begins with bringing celestial movements into alignment. A king establishes the starting point at the beginning, and therefore gives priority to determining the seasons; he assigns the remainder at the end, and therefore inserts intercalary months to complete the calendar. This also shows that the rulers and ministers of that time all understood Heaven and humanity and comprehended the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. In later ages, commonplace Confucian scholars have nothing to do with the calendar, while those who work on the calendar are not Confucian scholars. How can one expect them to understand it? Since the Xia dynasty, the offices of Xi and He have been combined into one; in later ages there have scarcely been officials specifically charged with these duties. How can one expect them to understand it?
“Be lenient yet maintain restraint; be unhurried and harmonious.”
Zhou Zongzheng
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Assistant Instructor: 〔What the sage calls leniency and harmony means that restraint is inherent in leniency, and an unhurried manner is inherent in harmony. Writers commonly take restraint as a corrective to leniency, and an unhurried manner as a corrective to harmony; this surely misses the point. This essay grasps it and should be selected for inclusion as a model of classical scholarship.〕
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: 〔When King Cheng commanded Jun Chen to succeed the Duke of Zhou after the latter’s cautious and vigilant administration, his precise intention was that Jun Chen should achieve good government through leniency and harmony. This essay brings out that meaning almost exhaustively.〕
Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor: 〔The writing has force and deserves recognition.〕
Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: 〔Reading this essay, one can discern the intention to establish the state upon loyalty and generosity.〕
Reflecting…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
賢王告大臣化殷之政惟在於寬和之適中也
蓋不同者時所貴因乎時者政也大臣化殷之
政不在於寬和之適中也哉成王命君陳尹東
郊告之至此若謂欲善天下之治當通天下之
變汝弘周公之丕訓宜何如哉彼東郊之民周
公嘗嚴以治之矣然濟其嚴者不在于寬乎汝
其無依勢也無倚法也本之於含弘廣大於善
惡無所不容行之以慈祥愷悌舉遠近皆在度
內可謂寬矣然一於寬不可也又必包含之中
===
凜然法制之依存惻怛之下森然品式之具備
師教于昔日者防閑之有法也保安于前人者
維持之有道也譬若大地之持載而規畫之剬
存焉寬以待民如此吾見其在周也猶在其殷
也豈復有迪屢不靖之梗化者哉下都之衆周
公嘗謹毖於始矣然繼其後者不在于和乎汝
其不作威也不以削也平易以近之譪然家人
父子之相親恩禮以待之宛乎手足頭目之相
愛可謂和矣然一于和不可也又必馴擾調娛
punctuated: 賢王告大臣化殷之政，惟在於寬和之適中也。蓋不同者時，所貴因乎時者政也。大臣化殷之政，不在於寬和之適中也哉？成王命君陳尹東郊，告之至此，若謂：「欲善天下之治，當通天下之變。汝弘周公之丕訓，宜何如哉？彼東郊之民，周公嘗嚴以治之矣。然濟其嚴者，不在于寬乎？汝其無依勢也，無倚法也，本之於含弘廣大，於善惡無所不容；行之以慈祥愷悌，舉遠近皆在度內，可謂寬矣。然一於寬不可也，又必包含之中，凜然法制之依存；惻怛之下，森然品式之具備。師教于昔日者，防閑之有法也；保安于前人者，維持之有道也。譬若大地之持載，而規畫之剬存焉。寬以待民如此，吾見其在周也，猶在其殷也，豈復有迪屢不靖之梗化者哉？下都之衆，周公嘗謹毖於始矣。然繼其後者，不在于和乎？汝其不作威也，不以削也，平易以近之，譪然家人父子之相親；恩禮以待之，宛乎手足頭目之相愛，可謂和矣。然一于和不可也，又必馴擾調娛
translation_en:
…the worthy king told his great minister that governing and transforming the people of Yin depended solely upon achieving the proper balance in generosity and harmony. For times differ, and what is valued in government is its adaptation to the times. Does not a great minister’s governance for transforming the people of Yin depend upon this proper balance in generosity and harmony?

When King Cheng appointed Jun Chen to govern the eastern outskirts and admonished him thus, it was as though he said: “To govern all under Heaven well, one must comprehend its changing circumstances. How should you extend the Duke of Zhou’s great teachings? The Duke of Zhou once governed the people of those eastern outskirts with severity. Yet does not tempering that severity depend upon generosity? Do not rely upon your power or lean upon the laws. Ground your conduct in broad-minded forbearance, accommodating both the good and the bad; act with kindness and amiability, embracing everyone, far and near, within your consideration. This may be called generosity. Yet generosity alone will not do. Within your forbearance, laws and institutions must remain an awe-inspiring presence; beneath your compassion, standards and regulations must stand fully arrayed. Following the instruction of former days [?] means having rules for restraint and prevention; preserving the security established by your predecessors means having a way to sustain it. This is like the great earth bearing all things, while the ordering of its divisions remains intact [?]. If you treat the people with such generosity, I see them living under Zhou as though they still lived under their own Yin. How could there again be anyone who repeatedly pursues unrest and obstructs transformation?

“The Duke of Zhou exercised caution and vigilance from the outset in dealing with the people of the lower capital. Yet does not carrying on after him depend upon harmony? Do not display overbearing authority or diminish the people’s means. Approach them with simplicity and ease, as affectionately as members of a household, fathers and sons, cherish one another. Treat them with kindness and ritual propriety, just as hands, feet, head, and eyes care for one another. This may be called harmony. Yet harmony alone will not do. You must also gently tame and soothe them…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
而從容乎道德之漸磨游息化養而厭飫乎禮
義之涵育弗若汝政者化誘之自如也弗化汝
訓者陶鎔之常在也譬若春風之長養而披拂
之力寓焉和以處民如此吾見夫在繼世也猶
夫在先王也又何有自作不典而撓治者哉吁
寬可能也寬而有制未易能也和可能也和而
從容未易能也達權濟變以成和中之治不有
望於汝君陳也耶嗟夫愚於是知周之所以處
殷民者至矣初命周公以師保之尊謹毖之繼
===
命君陳以寬和委曲化導之似亦未見其盡帖
然者至康王之時既歷三紀復命畢公以成終
之責保釐之然後世已變而風始移也嗚呼觀
其化之之難可以見殷之先王及民之德觀其
頑獷之性卒變爲良民又可以見周之先王化
民之仁
詩
鴥彼飛隼其飛戾天亦集爰止方叔涖止
其車三千師干之試方叔率止鉦人伐
punctuated:
而從容乎道德之漸磨，游息化養，而厭飫乎禮義之涵育。弗若汝政者，化誘之自如也；弗化汝訓者，陶鎔之常在也。譬若春風之長養，而披拂之力寓焉。和以處民如此，吾見夫在繼世也，猶夫在先王也，又何有自作不典而撓治者哉？吁！寬可能也，寬而有制未易能也；和可能也，和而從容未易能也。達權濟變，以成和中之治，不有望於汝君陳也耶？嗟夫！愚於是知周之所以處殷民者至矣。初命周公以師保之尊謹毖之，繼命君陳以寬和委曲化導之，似亦未見其盡帖然者。至康王之時，既歷三紀，復命畢公以成終之責保釐之，然後世已變而風始移也。嗚呼！觀其化之之難，可以見殷之先王及民之德；觀其頑獷之性卒變爲良民，又可以見周之先王化民之仁。

詩

鴥彼飛隼，其飛戾天，亦集爰止。方叔涖止，其車三千，師干之試。方叔率止，鉦人伐

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
鼓陳師鞠旅顯允方叔伐鼓淵淵振旅
闐闐
胡文宗
同考試官教諭許　批〔前後興詞俱在六句止而此興尤有意作者往往以衆盛有節對言且於進退之處蔽〕
〔於經文陳漏殊甚此作精練以昌其詞紆廻以發其趣知〕
〔非風擧篇章所能限也〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔師盛有節正見古人用兵多多益善處此作曲盡其意可錄〕
考試官教授吳　批〔文字嚴整且有步驟佳士佳〕
===
士
考試官教授王　批〔爲文亦有紀律〕
詩人興大將之師盛而有節而遂詳其實也蓋
行師之要以律爲臧也方叔爲將而進退有節
如此此其所以不戰而屈人之兵與釆芑之詩
宣王命方叔南征而軍士作此謂夫載瞻彼
之飛隼也上焉傅于天下焉翔而集勢不終于
飛也而有時乎止矣況我方叔之涖止也其車
punctuated:
鼓，陳師鞠旅。顯允方叔，伐鼓淵淵，振旅闐闐。
胡文宗
同考試官教諭許，批〔前後興詞俱在六句止，而此興尤有意。作者往往以衆盛有節對言，且於進退之處蔽〕〔於經文，陳漏殊甚。此作精練以昌其詞，紆廻以發其趣，知〕〔非風擧篇章所能限也。〕
同考試官教諭朱，批〔師盛有節，正見古人用兵多多益善處。此作曲盡其意，可錄。〕
考試官教授吳，批〔文字嚴整，且有步驟。佳士，佳士。〕
考試官教授王，批〔爲文亦有紀律。〕
詩人興大將之師盛而有節，而遂詳其實也。蓋行師之要，以律爲臧也。方叔爲將，而進退有節如此，此其所以不戰而屈人之兵與！釆芑之詩，宣王命方叔南征，而軍士作此，謂夫載瞻彼之飛隼也，上焉傅于天，下焉翔而集，勢不終于飛也，而有時乎止矣。況我方叔之涖止也，其車
translation_en:
…the drums; they array the troops and muster the companies. Illustrious and trustworthy is Fang Shu: the drums sound deep and resonant; the troops withdraw with a mighty din.
Hu Wenzong
Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “The evocative passages both before and after end at the sixth line, but this particular evocation is especially meaningful. Writers often discuss the army’s great numbers and its discipline as paired subjects; moreover, in treating advance and retreat, they are constrained by the canonical wording, with very serious deficiencies in exposition [?]. This composition is refined and concise, giving vigor to its language; its winding development brings out its meaning. Clearly it cannot be confined within the bounds of ‘fengju compositions’ [?].”
Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “The army’s great numbers and discipline show precisely why, in the ancients’ employment of troops, the more there were, the better. This composition fully explores that meaning and deserves selection.”
Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The writing is rigorous and orderly, and proceeds in measured stages. An excellent scholar, an excellent scholar!”
Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: “His composition, too, has discipline.”
The poet evokes the great commander’s numerous yet disciplined army, and then sets forth its actual circumstances in detail. For the essential principle of conducting an army is that discipline makes it good. As commander, Fang Shu maintained such order in advancing and retreating: was this not how he subdued the enemy’s forces without fighting? The poem Gathering Millet (Cai qi) was composed by the soldiers when King Xuan ordered Fang Shu to campaign in the south. Its meaning is this: look at that flying falcon. Above, it reaches the sky; below, it glides and settles. Its course does not consist solely of flight: there are also times when it comes to rest. How much more is this so when our Fang Shu arrives! His chariots…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
有三千之衆師干有練習之荚法不一干進也
而有時乎退焉故即其將戰而觀之我方叔之
率止也以爲兵雖多矣無制者敗于爲鉦人伐
鉦所以肅其選徒之警也鼓人伐鼓所以先其
赴敵之聲也既動鬩之又靜翕之而如山如川
之勢其在於斯乎兵雖練矣不令奚從于焉既
陳我師而昭其用命之誓復陳我旅而嚴以止
齊之規既三令之又五申之而攻城攻心之道
其出於是乎是則其將戰之有節也固如此又
===
即其始終而觀之彼顯允之方叔也以爲兵出
而無以治之則亂由是伐鼓淵淵使凡闐是聲
者勇者不必先而怯者不敢後同此行枚同此
聲討其視治兵也一視其將戰也旅入而無以
振之則散由是伐鼓闐闐使凡得於耳者前軍
無敢過後軍無不及以是結陳以是凱還其視
振旅也一視其治兵也是則其始終之有節也
又如此吁此方叔之兵所以先爲不可勝而蠻
荆之服正所以破其心與抑論之語曰君不擇
punctuated: 有三千之衆，師干有練習之荚，法不一干進也，而有時乎退焉。故即其將戰而觀之，我方叔之率止也，以爲兵雖多矣，無制者敗。于爲鉦人伐鉦，所以肅其選徒之警也；鼓人伐鼓，所以先其赴敵之聲也。既動鬩之，又靜翕之，而如山如川之勢，其在於斯乎！兵雖練矣，不令奚從？于焉既陳我師，而昭其用命之誓；復陳我旅，而嚴以止齊之規。既三令之，又五申之，而攻城攻心之道，其出於是乎！是則其將戰之有節也，固如此。又即其始終而觀之，彼顯允之方叔也，以爲兵出而無以治之則亂。由是伐鼓淵淵，使凡闐是聲者，勇者不必先，而怯者不敢後。同此行枚，同此聲討，其視治兵也，一視其將戰也。旅入而無以振之則散。由是伐鼓闐闐，使凡得於耳者，前軍無敢過，後軍無不及。以是結陳，以是凱還，其視振旅也，一視其治兵也。是則其始終之有節也，又如此。吁！此方叔之兵所以先爲不可勝，而蠻荆之服，正所以破其心與！抑論之，語曰：「君不擇
translation_en:
…numbered three thousand, and the troops possessed the benefit [?] of practiced training. Their methods did not consist solely in advancing [?]; at times they also withdrew. Thus, consider their preparations for battle. When our Fang Shu took command, he held that troops, however numerous, would suffer defeat without discipline. Accordingly [?], the gong officers struck their gongs to make the mustered soldiers heed the warning with solemn attention; the drum officers struck their drums to sound the signal before they charged the enemy. Now he stirred them to contention, now he quietly gathered them together: was this not what gave them the force of mountains and rivers? Though soldiers were trained, whose direction could they follow without orders? He therefore arrayed our hosts and made clear the oath to obey commands; he further arrayed our companies and enforced strict rules for halting and maintaining alignment. He ordered them three times and reiterated his commands five times: did not the means of attacking cities and overcoming hearts issue from this? Such, indeed, was his disciplined conduct when preparing for battle.

Consider, moreover, his conduct from beginning to end. That illustrious and trustworthy Fang Shu held that troops marching out would fall into disorder without proper regulation. He therefore had the drums beaten with a deep, resounding sound, so that among all who heard [?] it, the brave need not rush ahead and the timid dared not lag behind. All alike marched with mouth-gags [?]; all alike joined the punitive campaign. He treated the ordering of his troops just as he treated their preparations for battle. When the companies returned, they would disperse unless their ranks were put in order. He therefore had the drums beaten with a mighty din, so that among all who heard them, the vanguard dared not advance too far and the rearguard never fell short. In this way they formed their ranks; in this way they returned victorious. He treated the ordering of his returning troops just as he treated their ordering before departure. Such, moreover, was his discipline from beginning to end.

Ah! This was how Fang Shu’s troops first made themselves invincible; and was not the submission of the Man peoples of Jing precisely the result of breaking their will? To discuss the matter further, a saying runs: “If a ruler does not select…”

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
將以其國與敵也將不知兵以其主與敵也言
國之注於將也又曰有制之兵無能之將不可
以敗有能之將無制之兵不可以勝言將之繫
於制也今以方叔之威名而當征伐之重寄則
將與制固兩得之而宣王之善將將又可見矣
此其所以南征北伐而共成中興之業有以哉
雖然有宣王之知人然後有方叔之守法其道
則在乎上之人
受天之祜四方来賀
龔善治
===
同考試官教諭許　批　得天得人固嗣王繼先之效
寔武王裕後之休要之均一孝道之傳受也此作深得詩
人昭德規諷之旨錄之似可爲
今日
聖子神孫以孝嗣服之一助也
同考試官教諭朱　批　寫出有周世德之盛天人相
與之幾
考試官教授吳　批　詞意嚴整得作雅義之體
punctuated:
將，以其國與敵也；將不知兵，以其主與敵也。」言國之注於將也。又曰：「有制之兵，無能之將，不可以敗；有能之將，無制之兵，不可以勝。」言將之繫於制也。今以方叔之威名，而當征伐之重寄，則將與制固兩得之，而宣王之善將將又可見矣。此其所以南征北伐，而共成中興之業，有以哉！雖然，有宣王之知人，然後有方叔之守法，其道則在乎上之人。
受天之祜，四方来賀。
龔善治
同考試官教諭許批：得天得人，固嗣王繼先之效，寔武王裕後之休。要之，均一孝道之傳受也。此作深得詩人昭德規諷之旨，錄之似可爲今日聖子神孫以孝嗣服之一助也。
同考試官教諭朱批：寫出有周世德之盛，天人相與之幾。
考試官教授吳批：詞意嚴整，得作雅義之體。
translation_en:
…a commander, he hands his state over to the enemy; if a commander does not understand warfare, he hands his ruler over to the enemy.” This speaks of the state's dependence upon its commander. It is also said: “An army with proper regulations, though its commander lacks ability, cannot be defeated; an able commander with an army lacking regulations cannot win.” This speaks of the commander's dependence upon regulations. Now Fang Shu, with his prestige and renown, bore the weighty trust of conducting punitive campaigns: both the commander and the regulations were indeed fit for their purposes. Here too we can see King Xuan's skill in commanding commanders. There was good reason why they could campaign south and north and together accomplish the restoration of the dynasty! Nevertheless, only with King Xuan's discernment of men could there be Fang Shu's adherence to established rules. The way to achieve this thus rests with the ruler above.
“Receiving Heaven's blessings, he is congratulated by the four quarters.”
Gong Shanzhi
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: Winning Heaven's favor and the people's allegiance is indeed the result of the succeeding king's continuation of his forebears' work; it is also the blessing bestowed by King Wu in providing abundantly for his descendants. In essence, both are the transmission and reception of the same way of filial piety. This composition deeply grasps the poet's intent to manifest virtue and offer admonition through indirection. Recording it here may offer some assistance to the present day's sagely sons and divine grandsons in succeeding to the royal charge through filial piety.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor: It brings out the abundance of the Zhou dynasty's virtue accumulated through successive generations, and the subtle workings through which Heaven and humanity lend their support.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: Its diction and ideas are rigorous and orderly; it attains the proper form for an exposition of the meaning of the Odes of the Court.

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授王　批〔莊重典雅〕
詩人言後王繼先之效天與而人歸之也蓋天
福之所在人心之所在也後王以繼先而得之
前王裕後之休大矣哉詩人美武王能纘太王
王季文王之緒而有天下此則言其裕後之福
謂夫於皇武王達孝繼述乎先後餘休啓佑於
後昆來世而能纘承之則所以仰賴之者何既
邪是故世德之作求武王之孝通于神明者也
後世能襲之以爲守成之地則仰焉不愧於天
===
矣吾知天命雖難忱也感明德之惟馨隆休祥
以昭其行監宗子之惟肖覃福澤以厚其生安
富尊享之而未艾身之所履上帝其默相之
也祿位名壽保之於無窮事之所施鬼神其陰
隲之也以百行之原而遡皇天之福所以保佑
之者依然臨汝之成命矣天之與之後何減於
前耶天命既集人心焉之于京之克配武王之
孝光于四海者也後王能紹之以爲嗣統之規
則俯焉不怍於人矣吾知人心雖無常也覩君
punctuated:
考試官教授王批〔莊重典雅〕

詩人言後王繼先之效，天與而人歸之也。蓋天福之所在，人心之所在也。後王以繼先而得之，前王裕後之休大矣哉！詩人美武王能纘太王、王季、文王之緒而有天下，此則言其裕後之福。謂夫於皇武王，達孝繼述乎先後，餘休啓佑於後昆，來世而能纘承之，則所以仰賴之者何既邪？是故《世德》之作，求武王之孝通于神明者也。後世能襲之以爲守成之地，則仰焉不愧於天矣。吾知天命雖難忱也，感明德之惟馨，隆休祥以昭其行；監宗子之惟肖，覃福澤以厚其生。安富尊享之而未艾，身之所履，上帝其默相之也；祿位名壽保之於無窮，事之所施，鬼神其陰隲之也。以百行之原而遡皇天之福，所以保佑之者，依然臨汝之成命矣。天之與之，後何減於前耶？天命既集，人心焉之？于京之克配，武王之孝光于四海者也。後王能紹之以爲嗣統之規，則俯焉不怍於人矣。吾知人心雖無常也，覩君
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔Dignified and classically elegant.〕

The poet speaks of the results achieved by later kings in carrying on their predecessors’ work: Heaven supports them, and the people turn to them. For where Heaven’s blessings reside, there too reside the people’s hearts. Later kings obtain these by carrying on their predecessors’ work. How great, then, is the beneficence of former kings in providing for their successors! The poet praises King Wu for continuing the legacy of King Tai, Wang Ji, and King Wen and thereby possessing all under Heaven. Here, however, he speaks of the blessings King Wu provided for his successors. That august King Wu fulfilled his filial devotion by continuing the purposes and undertakings of the former rulers; his enduring beneficence opened the way for and protected his descendants. If later generations can carry on that legacy, how could the benefits on which they depend ever be exhausted? Thus the composition on “Generations of Virtue” (Shide) seeks to bring out how King Wu’s filial devotion reached the spirits. If later generations can inherit it as the foundation for preserving what has been accomplished, they can look upward without shame before Heaven.

I know that although Heaven’s Mandate is difficult to trust, Heaven responds to the fragrance of illustrious virtue, multiplying auspicious blessings to make manifest the ruler’s conduct. It observes that the heir to the ancestral line truly resembles his forebears, and extends blessings to enrich his life. Peace, wealth, and honor are enjoyed without end: in all that he personally undertakes, the Lord on High silently assists him. Emoluments, rank, renown, and longevity are preserved forever: in all the affairs he conducts, the spirits secretly secure his welfare. Through filial devotion, the source of all virtuous conduct, he reaches back to the blessings of august Heaven. What protects him remains that settled mandate which “looks down upon you.” How could Heaven’s support for later rulers be less than its support for earlier ones?

Once Heaven’s Mandate has converged upon him, where will the people’s hearts turn? The words “in the capital, able to match” refer to King Wu’s filial devotion shining throughout the Four Seas. If later kings can continue it as their rule for succeeding to the imperial line, they can look downward without shame before the people. I know that although the people’s hearts are inconstant, when they behold the ruler’s …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
德之重光而九州輸其誠悃仰世脩之弗替而
萬國動其歡心虞夏商周之胄奉玉帛而款以
周旋冊晨九重禮樂衣冠之會也文昭武穆之
親脩歲事而樂於趨附邦畿千里車書文軌之
宗也以天地之經而通天下之志所以愛戴之
者宛然媚茲之餘風矣人之歸之今何異於昔
邪是則一德之脩而天人交與武王之道垂貽
燕之澤者何如其悠久哉大抵人君之於天下
莫不由祖宗之脩德而樹立之亦莫不由子孫
===
之失德而陵夷之夏商之先皆以明德膺受天
命使其子孫繼而不衰則至今存矣周雖有代
德而命未改也奈何季叔不躅而上天西顧此
我周之所以繼興而二代之亡爲可惜也噫周
之子孫可不以是爲監而復使後人之惜周哉
春秋
春王正月〔隱公元年〕齊侯衛侯胥命于蒲
〔桓公三年〕
劉子忠
punctuated:
德之重光，而九州輸其誠悃；仰世脩之弗替，而萬國動其歡心。虞夏商周之胄，奉玉帛而款以周旋，冊晨九重，禮樂衣冠之會也。文昭武穆之親，脩歲事而樂於趨附，邦畿千里，車書文軌之宗也。以天地之經而通天下之志，所以愛戴之者，宛然媚茲之餘風矣。人之歸之，今何異於昔邪？是則一德之脩，而天人交與。武王之道垂貽燕之澤者，何如其悠久哉！大抵人君之於天下，莫不由祖宗之脩德而樹立之，亦莫不由子孫之失德而陵夷之。夏商之先，皆以明德膺受天命，使其子孫繼而不衰，則至今存矣。周雖有代德，而命未改也。奈何季叔不躅，而上天西顧？此我周之所以繼興，而二代之亡爲可惜也。噫！周之子孫，可不以是爲監，而復使後人之惜周哉？

春秋

春王正月〔隱公元年〕。齊侯、衛侯胥命于蒲〔桓公三年〕。

劉子忠
translation_en:
…the renewed brilliance of the ruler’s virtue, and the Nine Provinces offer their heartfelt sincerity; they look up to the unbroken cultivation of virtue through successive generations, and the myriad states are moved to delight. Descendants of Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou bear jade and silk and sincerely perform the ceremonial observances. Within the ninefold palace, amid court ceremonies [?], they assemble with rites and music, in ceremonial caps and robes. The royal kinsmen, arrayed in the zhao line of King Wen and the mu line of King Wu, perform the annual sacrifices and gladly come to attend. The royal domain, extending a thousand li, is the center of common standards for carriages, writing, culture, and wheel tracks. Through the enduring principles of Heaven and Earth, the aspirations of all under Heaven are brought into accord. Their love and allegiance preserve the lingering influence of the ancient injunction to cherish this ruler. How does the people’s allegiance today differ from that of old? Thus, through the cultivation of a single, consistent virtue, Heaven and humankind alike lend their support. How enduring is the Way of King Wu, passing down blessings of peace to his descendants!

Generally, rulers establish their dominion over all under Heaven through their ancestors’ cultivation of virtue; likewise, that dominion declines through their descendants’ loss of virtue. The forebears of Xia and Shang received Heaven’s Mandate through their luminous virtue. Had their descendants continued it without decline, those dynasties would still exist today. Although Zhou possessed the virtue to succeed them, the Mandate would not have changed. Yet why did Ji and Shu fail to follow the proper course [?], so that Heaven turned its gaze westward? This is why our Zhou arose to succeed them, and why the fall of the two dynasties is cause for regret. Alas! Can the descendants of Zhou fail to take this as a warning, and cause later generations in turn to lament Zhou?

Spring and Autumn Annals

“Spring, the first month of the king’s calendar.” 〔First year of Duke Yin.〕 “The Marquis of Qi and the Marquis of Wei mutually pledged their word at Pu.” 〔Third year of Duke Huan.〕

Liu Zizhong.

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導蔡　批　〔明聖人作春秋變周制處行者　多所未合此篇精切明簡足用錄出〕
同考試官教諭王　批　〔說法天道正人心處道理甚〕
大
考試官教授吳　批　〔發春秋盡易之　縕發忠明盡〕
考試官教授王　批　〔得聖人變周制之意〕
春秋變周制以從易有所以正時者有所以重
信者此見行夏時善胥命聖人無非用權以變
周制也其垂訓之旨深哉且仲冬周之正朔也
===
經於正月而書春然則正以仲冬者非耶蓋時
以作事而殷之建丑周之建子皆非所以授民
時也孰有時之正令之善如夏之建寅者乎建
諸天地質諸鬼神誠歷百王而無弊也春秋酌
先王之禮立萬世之法以治曆明時爲務於此
有待焉若曰月可周也事可魯也時不可以不
行乎夏也雖變周之制何惑焉故於隱之正月
特書春王以冠之殆與殷輅之乘韶舞之用同
一垂法後世之意也此義行則四時以定七政
punctuated:
同考試官訓導蔡　批：〔明聖人作春秋變周制處，行者多所未合，此篇精切明簡，足用錄出。〕
同考試官教諭王　批：〔說法天道正人心處，道理甚〕大。
考試官教授吳　批：〔發春秋盡易之縕，發忠明盡。〕
考試官教授王　批：〔得聖人變周制之意。〕
春秋變周制以從易，有所以正時者，有所以重信者。此見行夏時、善胥命，聖人無非用權以變周制也。其垂訓之旨深哉！且仲冬，周之正朔也。經於正月而書春，然則正以仲冬者非耶？蓋時以作事，而殷之建丑、周之建子，皆非所以授民時也。孰有時之正、令之善，如夏之建寅者乎？建諸天地，質諸鬼神，誠歷百王而無弊也。春秋酌先王之禮，立萬世之法，以治曆明時爲務，於此有待焉。若曰：月可周也，事可魯也，時不可以不行乎夏也。雖變周之制，何惑焉？故於隱之正月，特書春王以冠之，殆與殷輅之乘、韶舞之用，同一垂法後世之意也。此義行，則四時以定，七政
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Cai, an Assistant Instructor, comments: “In explaining where the Sage altered Zhou institutions in composing the Spring and Autumn Annals, current interpretations [?] often fail to accord with his meaning. This essay is precise and incisive, clear and concise, and merits inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Wang, an Instructor, comments: “The discussion of taking Heaven’s Way as a model and rectifying human hearts addresses principles of great scope.”

Examiner Wu, a Professor, comments: “It expounds how the Spring and Autumn Annals exhausts the profundities of the Book of Changes [?]; its exposition is faithful, clear, and exhaustive [?].”

Examiner Wang, a Professor, comments: “It grasps the Sage’s intention in altering Zhou institutions.”

The Spring and Autumn Annals alters Zhou institutions to accord with the Book of Changes: some alterations serve to rectify the seasons, others to give weight to trustworthiness. This is evident in its adoption of the Xia seasonal calendar and its approval of the mutual pledges. In both, the Sage exercised discretionary judgment to alter Zhou institutions. How profound was his purpose in leaving these teachings!

Now, midwinter was the beginning of the Zhou calendar year. Yet the Classic writes ‘spring’ alongside ‘the first month.’ Does this mean that beginning the year in midwinter was wrong? Seasons provide the timing for undertaking activities; neither the Yin practice of beginning the year in the month of chou nor the Zhou practice of beginning it in the month of zi properly served to communicate the seasons to the people. What could match the Xia practice of beginning the year in the month of yin for correctness of seasonal timing and excellence of ordinances? Established against Heaven and Earth and tested before ghosts and spirits, it could indeed endure through a hundred kings without defect. The Spring and Autumn Annals weighs the rites of former kings and establishes standards for all ages. Taking the regulation of the calendar and clarification of the seasons as its task, it looks to a future fulfillment in this matter. It is as though it said: ‘The numbering of months may follow Zhou; the events recorded may be those of Lu; but the seasons must follow Xia.’ Though this alters Zhou institutions, what cause is there for doubt?

Thus, before ‘the first month’ of Duke Yin’s reign, it specifically writes ‘spring, the king’s.’ This presumably expresses the same intention of leaving standards for later generations as the prescriptions to ride in the Yin state carriage and to employ the Shao dance. If this principle is put into practice, the four seasons will be fixed, and the seven celestial regulators …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
以齊欽若之治可繼無復事不師古而建亥者
矣若司盟周之秩官也經善胥命之不盟然則
官有司盟者非耶蓋信以發志而殷之作誓周
之作會皆非所以示民信也孰有言相結信相
諭如齊衛之胥命者乎意氣有孚盤瓔無設誠
曠百年而一見也夫子慨末世之僞志大道之
行以講信修睦爲事於此有取焉若曰食可去
也生可無也信不可以不同乎古也雖變周之
制無異焉故於齊衛之不盟特書胥命以善之
===
殆與尾屋之謹蕭魚之美同一見諸行事之驗
也此義行則不動而敬不言而信淳古之風可
四無復人愛其情而質于者矣吁時方建子變
之以建寅時方相盟變之以相命信非知權而
盡易者莫能與也然則春秋其空言哉大抵法
天者莫大乎時教民者莫先於信天道無形所
可見者時而已人心不同所可仗者信而已法
天以時則天德備乾之義也教民以信則人心
從中孚之義也然則夫子春與胥命之文豈直
punctuated: 以齊，欽若之治可繼，無復事不師古而建亥者矣。若司盟，周之秩官也，經善胥命之不盟，然則官有司盟者非耶？蓋信以發志，而殷之作誓、周之作會，皆非所以示民信也。孰有言相結、信相諭，如齊衛之胥命者乎？意氣有孚，盤瓔無設，誠曠百年而一見也。夫子慨末世之僞，志大道之行，以講信修睦爲事，於此有取焉。若曰：「食可去也，生可無也，信不可以不同乎古也。」雖變周之制，無異焉。故於齊衛之不盟，特書胥命以善之，殆與尾屋之謹、蕭魚之美，同一見諸行事之驗也。此義行，則不動而敬，不言而信，淳古之風可四，無復人愛其情而質于者矣。吁！時方建子，變之以建寅；時方相盟，變之以相命。信非知權而盡易者，莫能與也。然則《春秋》其空言哉？大抵法天者莫大乎時，教民者莫先於信。天道無形，所可見者時而已；人心不同，所可仗者信而已。法天以時，則天德備，《乾》之義也；教民以信，則人心從，《中孚》之義也。然則夫子春與胥命之文，豈直
translation_en:
…and thereby be brought into alignment. Government that reverently accords with Heaven could be continued, and there would no longer be those who failed to model their actions on antiquity and made the month of hai the beginning of the year.

As for the Director of Covenants, this was an established Zhou office. Yet the Classic praises the mutual pledging of Qi and Wei without a sworn covenant. Does this mean that having a Director of Covenants was wrong? Trustworthiness gives expression to intentions; yet neither the Shang practice of making oaths nor the Zhou practice of holding assemblies served to demonstrate trustworthiness to the people. What could compare with the mutual pledging of Qi and Wei, in which words bound the parties together and trustworthiness conveyed their intentions to one another? Their intentions and feelings were sincere, and no covenant vessels [?] were set out. Truly, this was something seen but once in a hundred years.

The Master lamented the deceit of a declining age and aspired to the realization of the Great Way. Taking the cultivation of trustworthiness and harmony as his task, he found something here worthy of adoption. It was as though he said: “Food may be dispensed with, and life may be surrendered, but trustworthiness must accord with antiquity.” Although this altered Zhou institutions, there was no departure from that principle. Thus, in recording that Qi and Wei did not swear a covenant, he specifically wrote “mutual pledging” to commend them. This presumably provides the same evidence in actual deeds as the care exercised at Weiwu [?] and the admirable conduct at Xiaoyu. Were this principle put into practice, people would command respect without acting and inspire trust without speaking. The simple customs of antiquity could be restored [?], and people would no longer conceal their true feelings and resort to pledges [?].

Ah! When the year began with the month of zi, he changed it to begin with yin; when people made sworn covenants with one another, he changed this to mutual pledging. Truly, only someone who understood discretionary judgment and fully comprehended change [?] could participate in this. Can the Spring and Autumn Annals, then, be mere empty words?

Generally, nothing is more important in modeling oneself on Heaven than the seasons, and nothing takes precedence over trustworthiness in teaching the people. Heaven’s Way has no form: what can be seen of it is simply the seasons. Human hearts differ: what can be relied upon is simply trustworthiness. To model oneself on Heaven through the seasons is to possess Heaven’s virtue in full: this is the meaning of the Qian hexagram, “The Creative.” To teach the people through trustworthiness is to secure the allegiance of their hearts: this is the meaning of the Zhongfu hexagram, “Inner Sincerity.” Thus, could the Master’s wording, “spring” and “mutual pledging,” be merely …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
魯史而已哉故曰聖人隨時變易以從道
冬十月甲午叔孫得臣敗狄于鹹〔文公十一年〕
阮范
同考試官訓導蔡　批〔題本平易作者不窘則泛是篇寫出聖人正名之意筆力峻健可以式矣〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔分别族類有制禦夷狄之意子能發之蓋深於經者〕
考試官教授吳　批〔發得正名意明淨〕
考試官教授王　批〔正名處須如此說方盡〕
===
即春秋紀狄之文見聖人正名之法夫春秋正
名之書也觀得臣敗狄之文槩可見矣思昔太
王有獯鬻之侵魯謳有膺懲之訓狄之為中國
患久矣春秋中葉暴横益張既潛師以侵齊遂
長驅而伐魯於是我公命將出師以禦門庭之
寇得臣分閫仗鉞以紓攘郤之謀一鼓而踣其
徒再鼓而奪其帥狄於是乎有鹹之敗焉春秋
直書其事何以見正名之法耶誠以統天下而
觀之一夷一夏不無内外美惡之分就夷狄而
punctuated:
魯史而已哉？故曰：聖人隨時變易以從道。

冬十月甲午，叔孫得臣敗狄于鹹。〔文公十一年〕
阮范

同考試官訓導蔡　批〔題本平易，作者不窘則泛。是篇寫出聖人正名之意，筆力峻健，可以式矣。〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔分别族類，有制禦夷狄之意，子能發之，蓋深於經者。〕
考試官教授吳　批〔發得正名意明淨。〕
考試官教授王　批〔正名處須如此說方盡。〕

即春秋紀狄之文，見聖人正名之法。夫春秋，正名之書也。觀得臣敗狄之文，槩可見矣。思昔太王有獯鬻之侵，魯謳有膺懲之訓，狄之為中國患久矣。春秋中葉，暴横益張，既潛師以侵齊，遂長驅而伐魯。於是我公命將出師，以禦門庭之寇。得臣分閫仗鉞，以紓攘郤之謀，一鼓而踣其徒，再鼓而奪其帥，狄於是乎有鹹之敗焉。春秋直書其事，何以見正名之法耶？誠以統天下而觀之，一夷一夏，不無内外美惡之分；就夷狄而
translation_en:
…merely the annals of Lu? Thus it is said: the sage adapts to changing times in order to follow the Way.

“In winter, in the tenth month, on the jiawu day, Shusun Dechen defeated the Di at Xian.” 〔Eleventh year of Duke Wen〕
Ruan Fan

Associate Examiner Cai, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The topic is straightforward, but writers tend either to feel constrained or to become diffuse. This essay brings out the sage’s intention of rectifying names. Its brushwork is forceful and vigorous; it can serve as a model.〕
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: 〔Distinguishing peoples by their kind conveys the intention of controlling and resisting the Yi and Di. You have been able to bring this out, showing profound understanding of the Classic.〕
Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: 〔The meaning of rectifying names is brought out clearly and cleanly.〕
Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: 〔The rectification of names must be explained in this way if its meaning is to be fully expressed.〕

In the Spring and Autumn Annals’ record of the Di, we see the sage’s method of rectifying names. The Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that rectifies names. Its general purport can be seen in the passage recording Dechen’s defeat of the Di. Consider how, in ancient times, King Tai suffered invasion by the Xunyu, and how the hymns of Lu contain an admonition to strike and punish them. The Di have long been a source of trouble for the central states. In the middle of the Spring and Autumn period, their violence and arrogance grew ever greater. Having secretly dispatched troops to invade Qi, they then drove deep into Lu to attack it. Thereupon our duke ordered a commander to lead out the army and resist the invaders at our very gates. Dechen assumed independent military command and took up the battle-axe of authority to carry out his plan for repelling them [?]. At the first beating of the drums he laid their troops low; at the second he captured their commander. Thus the Di suffered their defeat at Xian. The Spring and Autumn Annals records the event directly: how does this reveal the method of rectifying names? Indeed, viewed in terms of all under Heaven, the Yi and the Xia are distinguished as outer and inner, bad and good; considered among the Yi and Di themselves …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
論之其地其人不無大小强弱之異故在我之
界限既不可以不嚴而在彼之種類亦不容以
不別今狄也不守北方之巢穴敢與大國以抗
衡其狼貪虎噬之心非若勢狄之效順猶有所
慕而朝也其跋扈跳梁之勢非若赤狄之寡弱
猶可得撲而滅也雖見挫於今不容無防於其
後雖幸勝於魯不能恒保於其他聖人於此本
其實正其名直以狄書而别於白狄赤狄云者
蓋以無心之文寓有心之法使後之人知此狄
===
蓋嘗侵齊者也蓋嘗伐魯者也蓋屢爲中國患
者也則名以考其地因地以察其人隨其大小
强弱之勢以立吾禦之之法則聖人之意得矣
雖然狄固不足責也使文公能倚於法家拂士
以德脩國政得臣能急於責難陳善以禮格君
心則國勢又安外憂不作何狄人之敢伐哉君
以苟安爲志臣以幸勝爲功上下嬉嬉而胥日
不競矣聖人本其詐戰而以敗書意者深著胥
國君臣之罪以爲好武功而不脩文德者戒歟
punctuated:
論之，其地其人，不無大小强弱之異。故在我之界限，既不可以不嚴，而在彼之種類，亦不容以不別。今狄也，不守北方之巢穴，敢與大國以抗衡。其狼貪虎噬之心，非若勢狄之效順，猶有所慕而朝也；其跋扈跳梁之勢，非若赤狄之寡弱，猶可得撲而滅也。雖見挫於今，不容無防於其後；雖幸勝於魯，不能恒保於其他。聖人於此，本其實，正其名，直以狄書，而别於白狄、赤狄云者，蓋以無心之文寓有心之法，使後之人知此狄，蓋嘗侵齊者也，蓋嘗伐魯者也，蓋屢爲中國患者也。則名以考其地，因地以察其人，隨其大小强弱之勢，以立吾禦之之法，則聖人之意得矣。

雖然，狄固不足責也。使文公能倚於法家拂士，以德脩國政；得臣能急於責難陳善，以禮格君心，則國勢又安，外憂不作，何狄人之敢伐哉？君以苟安爲志，臣以幸勝爲功，上下嬉嬉，而胥日不競矣。聖人本其詐戰而以敗書，意者深著胥國君臣之罪，以爲好武功而不脩文德者戒歟？
translation_en:
…considered among themselves, their territories and peoples differ in size and strength. Thus, while the boundary on our side must be strictly maintained, the distinctions among their groups must also be recognized. These Di, instead of remaining in their northern lairs, dared to contend with a great state. Their wolfish greed and tigerish voracity were unlike the submission of the Shi Di [?], who still had something they admired and therefore came to court. Their insolent and unruly power was unlike the weakness and small numbers of the Chi Di, who could still be struck down and destroyed. Although checked now, they must still be guarded against in the future; although Lu fortunately defeated them, such success cannot always be assured elsewhere. Here the Sage based himself on the facts and rectified the designation, recording them simply as “Di,” distinguishing them from those called Bai Di and Chi Di. In apparently dispassionate wording he embedded a deliberate rule, so that later generations would know that these Di were those who had invaded Qi, those who had attacked Lu, and those who had repeatedly afflicted the Central States. By using the designation to investigate their territory, and their territory to examine their people, we can establish methods of resisting them suited to their size and strength. In this way, the Sage’s intention is understood.

Even so, the Di hardly warrant reproach. Had Duke Wen relied on families versed in the laws and ministers who would correct him, cultivating the government of his state through virtue; and had Dechen made it his urgent concern to demand difficult achievements of his ruler and set goodness before him, rectifying the ruler’s heart through ritual propriety, then the state would have been secure and external troubles would not have arisen. How would the Di have dared to attack? The ruler sought only ease for the moment, and his minister counted a lucky victory as an achievement. Those above and below idled in pleasure, and together grew weaker by the day [?]. Taking account of their deceitful warfare, the Sage recorded the event with the word “defeated.” Was his intention perhaps to expose fully the guilt of the ruler and ministers of the state [?], as a warning to those who delight in martial achievements but fail to cultivate civil virtue?

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
禮記
郊特牲而社稷大牢天子適諸侯諸侯膳
用犢諸侯適天子天子賜之禮大牢貴
誠之義也
黄溥
同考試官教諭陳　批　善發揮以少爲貴之意
考試官教授吳　批　辭理明整
考試官教授王　批　有文藻
記者詳禮之以少爲貴者而必有其義也甚矣
===
禮之所貴者誠也則夫郊祀之所用與天子之
所膳者得非以此義歟想其意謂夫禮必有義
而其大者唯誠巳矣是故饗帝曰郊郊禮之重
者也禮重則心肅故天子之郊也大報天之事
而就陽位以求其格者薦惟一牛而巳至若社
稷三獻之祀輕則祭以大牢而駿奔于祼亦彰
功德之報矣奉君曰膳膳禮之至者也禮至則
敬深故天子之出也入諸侯之境而列盆盎以
致其養者牲亦用犢而巳若夫人臣來朝之禮
punctuated:
禮記

「郊特牲，而社稷大牢；天子適諸侯，諸侯膳用犢；諸侯適天子，天子賜之禮大牢。貴誠之義也。」

黄溥

同考試官教諭陳批：「善發揮以少爲貴之意。」
考試官教授吳批：「辭理明整。」
考試官教授王批：「有文藻。」

記者詳禮之以少爲貴者，而必有其義也。甚矣，禮之所貴者誠也！則夫郊祀之所用與天子之所膳者，得非以此義歟？想其意謂夫禮必有義，而其大者唯誠巳矣。是故饗帝曰郊，郊禮之重者也。禮重則心肅，故天子之郊也，大報天之事，而就陽位以求其格者，薦惟一牛而巳。至若社稷，三獻之祀輕，則祭以大牢，而駿奔于祼，亦彰功德之報矣。奉君曰膳，膳禮之至者也。禮至則敬深，故天子之出也，入諸侯之境，而列盆盎以致其養者，牲亦用犢而巳。若夫人臣來朝之禮
translation_en:
Record of Rites (Liji)

“At the suburban sacrifice, a single animal is offered; at sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain, a full offering of ox, sheep, and pig is used. When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, they serve him a calf; when the feudal lords visit the Son of Heaven, he honors them with a full offering of ox, sheep, and pig. This expresses the principle of valuing sincerity.”

Huang Pu 黄溥

Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “Skillfully develops the meaning of valuing fewer offerings.”
Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The language and reasoning are clear and orderly.”
Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: “Has literary elegance.”

The compiler of the Record details those instances in ritual where fewer offerings are esteemed, and these must have their underlying principle. How paramount is sincerity among the things that ritual esteems! Could the offerings used in the suburban sacrifice and the food served to the Son of Heaven fail to embody this principle? I take his meaning to be that ritual necessarily has an underlying principle, and that its greatest principle is simply sincerity. Thus, offering to the Supreme Lord is called the suburban sacrifice; this is among the weightiest rites. When the rite is weighty, the heart is solemn. Hence, when the Son of Heaven performs the suburban sacrifice, undertaking the great act of requiting Heaven and approaching the position of yang to seek its coming, he presents only a single ox. As for the altars of soil and grain, their sacrifice with three presentations is less weighty, so a full offering of ox, sheep, and pig is sacrificed. Hastening to perform the libation also manifests recompense for their achievements and beneficence.

Serving the ruler food is called providing a meal; this is among the most exalted rites. When the rite is exalted, reverence is profound. Hence, when the Son of Heaven travels and enters the territory of a feudal lord, those who arrange the bowls and jars to provide his sustenance likewise use only a calf as the sacrificial animal. As for the rites when a subject comes to court …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
降則撫以太牢而升殺于俎肆亦大君之慈矣
夫若是者何哉蓋天遠而難格事之以多品不
若事之以誠敬之爲至茲特牲用於郊祀而不
用於社稷者非儉於物也重情實之未啓而爾
粟之純有以妙造化之誠品物簡而精神通一
二簋用享之遺意也昭格之義斯其至乎人君
其尊如天奉之以彌文不若奉之以忠懿之爲
極故犢獻於天子而不以賜於諸臣者亦非嗇
于禮也貴牝牡之未分而童牛之眞有以凝陰
===
陽之會物味薄而禮意渥一玄酒太羹之餘意
也享獻之義舍此何以哉是則誠有所當隆而
禮不以少爲嫌人臣之尊君亦猶君之尊天如
此先王之教微矣雖然禮也者所以式敬也名
也者所以定分也先王生人之道必與之以敬
以分者何邪蓋非敬則褻褻則流非分則僭僭
則亂褻與流僭與亂其禮之偷亡之漸乎故先
王恥流而生亂也則爲之立禮以昭其分爲之
存誠以久其敬防患之意蓋有出於報功報德
punctuated:
降，則撫以太牢，而升殺于俎肆，亦大君之慈矣。夫若是者何哉？蓋天遠而難格，事之以多品，不若事之以誠敬之爲至。茲特牲用於郊祀而不用於社稷者，非儉於物也，重情實之未啓，而爾粟之純有以妙造化之誠。品物簡而精神通，一二簋用享之遺意也。昭格之義，斯其至乎！人君其尊如天，奉之以彌文，不若奉之以忠懿之爲極。故犢獻於天子而不以賜於諸臣者，亦非嗇于禮也，貴牝牡之未分，而童牛之眞有以凝陰陽之會。物味薄而禮意渥，一玄酒太羹之餘意也。享獻之義，舍此何以哉？是則誠有所當隆，而禮不以少爲嫌。人臣之尊君，亦猶君之尊天如此，先王之教微矣。

雖然，禮也者，所以式敬也；名也者，所以定分也。先王生人之道，必與之以敬以分者，何邪？蓋非敬則褻，褻則流；非分則僭，僭則亂。褻與流，僭與亂，其禮之偷亡之漸乎？故先王恥流而生亂也，則爲之立禮以昭其分，爲之存誠以久其敬。防患之意，蓋有出於報功報德
translation_en:
…is of a lower order, they are graciously entertained with the full sacrificial complement of ox, sheep, and pig. The slaughtered animals are set upon the offering stands and arrayed there: this too expresses the great ruler’s benevolence. Why is this so? Heaven is distant and difficult to bring to respond. Serving it with many kinds of offerings is less perfect than serving it with sincerity and reverence. That a single animal is used in the suburban sacrifice to Heaven, but not in sacrifices to the gods of soil and grain, is no attempt to economize on material offerings. It values genuine feeling before its unfolding; the purity of “er su” [?] wondrously embodies the sincerity of creation’s transformations. The offerings are simple, yet spiritual communion is achieved. This preserves the meaning of presenting an offering with just two gui vessels [?]. Surely here the principle of eliciting the spirits’ manifest presence reaches its highest expression!

The ruler is as exalted as Heaven. Serving him with elaborate ceremony is less consummate than serving him with loyalty and goodness. Thus, presenting a calf to the Son of Heaven, while not bestowing one upon his ministers, likewise does not mean stinting on ritual. It prizes the stage before male and female are differentiated, when the unspoiled nature of the young ox can embody the conjunction of yin and yang. The offerings are scant in flavor, but rich in ritual meaning. This preserves the intention behind “dark liquor”—plain water—and the unseasoned broth [?]. Apart from this, wherein could the meaning of sacrificial presentation lie? Thus sincerity must receive its due emphasis, and ritual need not be faulted for the smallness of its offerings. A minister’s honoring of his ruler is just like the ruler’s honoring of Heaven in this respect. How subtle was the teaching of the former kings!

Nevertheless, ritual provides a form for reverence, and titles establish distinctions of rank. Why did the former kings, in their way of nurturing the people, necessarily furnish them with both reverence and distinctions of rank? Without reverence there is disrespect, and disrespect leads to unrestrained conduct; without distinctions of rank there is usurpation, and usurpation leads to disorder. Are not disrespect and unrestrained conduct, usurpation and disorder, the successive stages by which ritual becomes lax and disappears? Thus the former kings regarded it as shameful that unrestrained conduct should produce disorder. They established ritual to make distinctions of rank clear, and preserved sincerity to make reverence endure. Their intention in guarding against trouble surely extended beyond repaying achievements and rewarding virtue…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
之外者君子其知之乎
宮爲君商爲臣角爲民徵爲事羽爲物
畢竟兒蔑
同考試官教諭陳　批〔五聲於君臣民事物非止爲象而寔有通貫之妙此作獨精到明暢是宜錄出〕
考試官教授吳　批〔說出道即器器即道意義著得者〕
考試官教授王　批〔文思精緻〕
論樂聲之妙而寓人道之大焉夫樂也者象倫
===
者也惟聲音之見於樂者有寓於人之道則可
以知政矣樂記君子謂夫樂以妙天道於無形
聲以闡人道於有象蓋五聲之始有所謂宮者
厥音屬土而統乎律呂之元其聲至濁而起於
黃鍾之度是則五聲之獨尊者也其有君道乎
蓋君也者刑于百辟而建有極之中憲于萬邦
而端作孚之體然則宮之主於衆音也其猶君
之宰於萬化者耶商之爲聲也生於徵之三分
而益一得數七十而有二屬乎金而聲之次濁
punctuated:
之外者，君子其知之乎？

宮爲君，商爲臣，角爲民，徵爲事，羽爲物。
畢竟兒蔑
同考試官教諭陳　批〔五聲於君臣民事物，非止爲象，而寔有通貫之妙。此作獨精到明暢，是宜錄出。〕
考試官教授吳　批〔說出道即器、器即道意義，著得者。〕
考試官教授王　批〔文思精緻。〕

論樂聲之妙，而寓人道之大焉。夫樂也者，象倫者也。惟聲音之見於樂者，有寓於人之道，則可以知政矣。《樂記》君子謂夫樂以妙天道於無形，聲以闡人道於有象。蓋五聲之始，有所謂宮者，厥音屬土，而統乎律呂之元；其聲至濁，而起於黃鍾之度。是則五聲之獨尊者也，其有君道乎？蓋君也者，刑于百辟，而建有極之中；憲于萬邦，而端作孚之體。然則宮之主於衆音也，其猶君之宰於萬化者耶？商之爲聲也，生於徵之三分而益一，得數七十而有二，屬乎金而聲之次濁。
translation_en:
…beyond these: does the gentleman understand this?

“Gong represents the ruler; shang, the ministers; jue, the people; zhi, affairs; and yu, things.”
Bi Jing'er Mie [?; the transcription of this apparent name is doubtful].
Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: 〔The five tones do more than symbolize the ruler, ministers, people, affairs, and things: there is indeed a subtle coherence running through them. This composition is exceptionally precise, lucid, and fluent, and deserves to be selected for inclusion.〕
Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: 〔It brings out the meaning of “the Way is concrete things, and concrete things are the Way.” This is writing that succeeds [?].〕
Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: 〔The conception of the essay is refined.〕

In discussing the subtlety of musical tones, one finds embodied therein the greatness of the human Way. Music represents the ordered relationships of human life. Since the sounds manifested in music embody the Way governing human beings, through them one can understand government. The gentleman of the Record of Music holds that music gives subtle expression to the Way of Heaven in the formless, while sound elucidates the human Way through perceptible manifestations.

At the beginning of the five tones is what is called gong. Its tone belongs to Earth and presides over the source of the pitch standards. Its sound is the deepest, and it originates in the measure of the Huangzhong pitch pipe. Thus it alone occupies the position of highest honor among the five tones. Does it not possess the Way of the ruler? The ruler provides a model for the hundred officials and establishes the central standard; he serves as an exemplar for the myriad states and rectifies his own person as the embodiment of trustworthiness. Is gong’s mastery over the other tones not, then, like the ruler’s governance of the myriad transformations?

As a tone, shang is generated by dividing the measure of zhi into three and adding one such part, yielding the number seventy-two. It belongs to Metal, and its sound is the next deepest…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
誠是矣然日纏有自然之度而以已意附
之可乎故虞劇嘗曰朔在會同苟纏次既
合何疑於頻大日月相離何拘於間小一
行亦曰天事誠密雖四大三小庸何傷郭
守敬祖用其說一以辰集時刻所在之日
爲定朔夫定朔立則交會之時日不紊矣
交會準則天運之先後可驗矣二者相因
而不可失一者也我
朝大統曆法悉用授時曆之制洪武中漏刻
===
博士元統節取其法以洪武十七年甲子
爲曆元其實因之而未嘗改也迄今百五
十餘年行之而無弊近年以來因交食之
際有先天後天之不同而不能一一密合
議者遂謂其法已久不能無差而欲增損
之者愚以爲得其人則可不得其人恐未
可輕議也蓋嘗讀元史李謙曆議而玩其
測驗之法自近日以至遠日自近地以至
遠地東極高麗西極滇地南踰朱崖北盡
punctuated:
誠是矣，然日纏有自然之度，而以已意附之，可乎？故虞劇嘗曰：「朔在會同，苟纏次既合，何疑於頻大？日月相離，何拘於間小？」一行亦曰：「天事誠密，雖四大三小，庸何傷？」郭守敬祖用其說，一以辰集時刻所在之日爲定朔。夫定朔立，則交會之時日不紊矣；交會準，則天運之先後可驗矣。二者相因而不可失一者也。
我朝大統曆法悉用授時曆之制。洪武中，漏刻博士元統節取其法，以洪武十七年甲子爲曆元，其實因之而未嘗改也。迄今百五十餘年，行之而無弊。近年以來，因交食之際有先天後天之不同，而不能一一密合，議者遂謂其法已久，不能無差，而欲增損之者。愚以爲，得其人則可；不得其人，恐未可輕議也。蓋嘗讀元史李謙曆議，而玩其測驗之法，自近日以至遠日，自近地以至遠地，東極高麗，西極滇地，南踰朱崖，北盡
translation_en:
…That is indeed so. Yet the sun’s motion has its natural measures: can one impose one’s own notions upon it? Thus Yu Ju [?] once said: “The new moon occurs at conjunction. If the celestial positions coincide, why doubt the occurrence of consecutive long months? When the sun and moon are separated, why insist on interspersing short months?” Yixing likewise said: “If the reckoning of celestial phenomena is truly exact, what harm is there even in four long months or three short months in succession?” Guo Shoujing adopted this reasoning, determining the true new moon solely by the day on which the precise moment of conjunction [?] fell. Once the true new moon is established, the dates and times of conjunction are no longer confused; once conjunctions are accurately determined, advances and delays in celestial motion can be verified. These two depend upon each other, and neither can be dispensed with.
Our dynasty’s Grand Concordance Calendar follows entirely the system of the Season-Granting Calendar. During the Hongwu reign, Yuan Tong, Erudite of the Clepsydra, selected and adapted its methods, taking the seventeenth year of Hongwu, a jiazi year [1384], as the calendrical epoch. In substance, he continued its methods without changing them. For more than 150 years down to the present, they have been used without fault. In recent years, however, predicted eclipse times have sometimes preceded and sometimes followed the actual celestial events, failing to agree precisely in every instance. Those discussing the matter consequently maintain that the methods, having been in use so long, cannot be free of error, and some wish to amend them. In my humble opinion, this is permissible if the right person can be found; without such a person, I fear that revision should not be lightly proposed. I have read Li Qian’s discussion of calendrical methods in the History of the Yuan and pondered its procedures for observation and verification. They extended from observations of the sun nearby to those far away [?], and from nearby places to distant ones: eastward as far as Gaoli, westward as far as Dian, southward beyond Zhuya, and northward all the way to…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
鐵勒不可謂不精矣而又上考往古自春
秋獻公以來二千一百六十餘年打其增𦚾
合不可謂不密矣何所據而增損之若或
者又疑元統有年遠數盈漸差天度之說
殊不知所謂歲差云者指冬至日纏赤道
之度耳是故當改者也非謂氣朔也氣朔
不可改也若曰天運難測或有未盡之數
久而方覺則其要又在乎測驗而已今許
衡郭守敬所造簡儀仰儀及諸儀表之制
===
具載於史或可做而行之否乎雖然愚又
有說焉戴記有曰聖人有國則日月不食
星辰不勃朱子曰王者修德行政用賢去
姦能使陽盛足以勝陰則月常避日而不
食是或一道也君天下者於日月之薄蝕
豈可一諉於數哉愚也草茅下士素無師
傳姑舉經史所載者云爾而未敢以爲然
也惟執事進教之
第四問
punctuated:
鐵勒，不可謂不精矣。而又上考往古，自春秋獻公以來二千一百六十餘年，打其增𦚾合，不可謂不密矣。何所據而增損之？若或者又疑元統有年遠數盈、漸差天度之說，殊不知所謂歲差云者，指冬至日纏赤道之度耳。是故當改者也，非謂氣朔也，氣朔不可改也。若曰天運難測，或有未盡之數，久而方覺，則其要又在乎測驗而已。今許衡、郭守敬所造簡儀、仰儀及諸儀表之制，具載於史，或可做而行之否乎？雖然，愚又有說焉。《戴記》有曰：「聖人有國，則日月不食，星辰不勃。」朱子曰：「王者修德行政，用賢去姦，能使陽盛足以勝陰，則月常避日而不食。」是或一道也。君天下者，於日月之薄蝕，豈可一諉於數哉？愚也，草茅下士，素無師傳，姑舉經史所載者云爾，而未敢以爲然也。惟執事進教之。

第四問
translation_en:
…as far as Tiele. These observations can hardly be called imprecise. Moreover, they investigated antiquity, examining more than 2,160 years from the time of Duke Xian in the Spring and Autumn period onward, checking increases and agreement [?]. This can hardly be called insufficiently exact. On what grounds, then, should adjustments be made? Some may still harbor doubts because Yuan Tong spoke of numerical excess accumulating over the years and gradually diverging from the celestial positions. They fail to understand that what is called annual precession refers only to the degree of the sun’s position on the celestial equator at the winter solstice. This, therefore, is what should be adjusted; it does not refer to the solar terms and new moons. The solar terms and new moons must not be altered. If one says that celestial motion is difficult to fathom and that some numerical factors may remain unaccounted for, becoming apparent only after a long time, then the essential requirement is simply observation and verification. The designs of the simplified instrument, the upward-facing instrument, and the other instruments and gnomons constructed by Xu Heng and Guo Shoujing are fully recorded in the histories. Might these be reproduced and put into use?

Nevertheless, I have another point to offer. The Record of Rites of Dai states: “When a sage possesses a state, the sun and moon suffer no eclipses, and the stars fall into no disorder.” Master Zhu said: “If a ruler cultivates virtue and carries out good government, employs the worthy and removes the wicked, he can make yang flourish sufficiently to overcome yin; then the moon will always avoid the sun, and no eclipse will occur.” This may be another way. How could one who rules all under Heaven attribute eclipses of the sun and moon entirely to numerical regularities? I am but a humble scholar outside official life, who has never received instruction from a master. I have merely adduced what is recorded in the classics and histories and do not dare assert that my conclusions are correct. I ask only that you, honored examiners, further instruct me.

Fourth Question

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄

阮范
同考試官訓導蔡　批　周禮迺經世大典我
國家稽古建官多所取法宜乎致文明之治矣但其書湮沒已久不獲盡傳不
及一子史之行世可勝惜哉子能张拯底蘊敷吝詳明蓋
悉所以崇信之道取用之方直破千載固陋之疑非□□於

阮范

同考試官訓導蔡批：周禮迺經世大典，我國家稽古建官，多所取法，宜乎致文明之治矣。但其書湮沒已久，不獲盡傳，不及一子史之行世，可勝惜哉！子能张拯底蘊，敷吝詳明，蓋悉所以崇信之道、取用之方，直破千載固陋之疑，非□□於用世者而能若是乎？

尊聖人之經者，當信其人而不疑其小迹。□人之法者，惟師其意而不泥其迹。蓋迹不可泥，而小者不必疑也。不泥較而疑將
translation_en:
Ruan Fan 阮范

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Assistant Instructor: The Rites of Zhou is a great canon for governing the world. In establishing offices through study of antiquity, our dynasty has drawn extensively upon it as a model; it is fitting that this should have brought about enlightened government. Yet the book has long suffered obscurity and loss and has not been transmitted in its entirety. Its circulation does not even equal that of a single work of the philosophical masters or historians. How deeply regrettable! You can bring out its underlying meaning [?] and expound it clearly and in detail [?], fully explaining how to honor and trust it and how to put it to use. You directly dispel the doubts born of narrow understanding over a thousand years. Could anyone who was not [two illegible characters] in practical statecraft accomplish this?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: The spirit and methods of mind of the Duke of Zhou are all contained in the single book Offices of Zhou—precisely what Confucius meant by being “set forth on wooden tablets and bamboo slips.” Your understanding that it can assuredly be taken as a model and put into practice is such that you must know how to place firm trust in the Duke of Zhou and Confucius!

Comment by Examiner [name illegible], Professor: [Four illegible characters] to doubt the people of Zhou on account of the strained interpretations of Han scholars. [Eighteen illegible characters] can [four illegible characters] and achieve conspicuous results amid the welter of competing explanations [?].

Those who revere the sage's canon should trust the man and not doubt the minor details of his deeds. Those who [illegible] the man's methods should take his intentions as their model without clinging to the outward traces of his deeds. For one must not cling to those traces, and minor details need not be doubted. “Not clinging, comparing, and doubting” [?] will …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
亦其可信者棄之矣縱小功之不察而庶
二年可乎不可況而況將亦其可師者求
之矣一啊之不下而廢朝夕可乎今夫聖
遠不幸不見其盛猶幸得見其書其今篇
大義閎炳炳在也而世遂謂殘不能一一
盡信者勢也或謝以皎知或補以就正皆
是也可因小而盡疑其大哉其大經大法
又磐磐可行也而時異勢殊不能一一深
同者亦勢也或酌之而準今或通之以合
===
俗亦宜也可況迹而不師其意乎夫然則
可以讀天下之書論天下之事而一無難
處者矣況周禮之書之大尤當講求而法
行者乎敢因明問而陳其槩夫周禮者聖
人經世之書也周公以其盡倫之體而爲
盡制之用本乎內聖之學而爲外王之規
上自黃帝以迄二代順風氣之宜因時勢
之變斟酌而損益之蓋集百聖之大成立
一王之定制觀其篇首每曰惟王建國辨
punctuated: 亦其可信者棄之矣。縱小功之不察而庶二年，可乎？不可。況而況將亦其可師者求之矣。一啊之不下而廢朝夕，可乎？今夫聖遠，不幸不見其盛，猶幸得見其書。其今篇大義，閎炳炳在也，而世遂謂殘，不能一一盡信者，勢也。或謝以皎知，或補以就正，皆是也。可因小而盡疑其大哉？其大經大法，又磐磐可行也，而時異勢殊，不能一一深同者，亦勢也。或酌之而準今，或通之以合俗，亦宜也。可況迹而不師其意乎？夫然則可以讀天下之書，論天下之事，而一無難處者矣。況周禮之書之大，尤當講求而法行者乎？敢因明問而陳其槩。夫周禮者，聖人經世之書也。周公以其盡倫之體，而爲盡制之用，本乎內聖之學，而爲外王之規。上自黃帝以迄二代，順風氣之宜，因時勢之變，斟酌而損益之，蓋集百聖之大成，立一王之定制。觀其篇首，每曰：「惟王建國，辨
translation_en: …one would discard even what is trustworthy in it. Could one, through failing to examine a minor achievement, then “hope for two years” [?]? One could not. Still more, one would also seek in it what could serve as a model [?]. Could one abandon morning and evening because “a single ah does not descend” [?]? Now the sages are far removed from us. Unfortunate though we are not to have witnessed their flourishing age, we are nevertheless fortunate to see their writings. The great principles of the surviving chapters [?] remain grand and brilliantly manifest. Yet people call the text fragmentary; that not every detail can be fully trusted follows from the circumstances. Whether one acknowledges a lack of clear understanding [?] or supplies what is missing to arrive at a correct text, either course is right. But can one doubt everything great in it on account of something small? Its great guiding principles and institutions are also firmly established and practicable. Yet times and circumstances differ, so that not every detail can coincide precisely: this too follows from the circumstances. It is likewise fitting either to weigh its provisions against present conditions or to adapt them to accord with prevailing customs. Can one dwell on its outward traces [?] and fail to take its underlying intent as a model? Proceeding in this way, one could read the books of the world and discuss its affairs without encountering anything impossible to resolve. How much more does this apply to a book as great as the Rites of Zhou, which especially deserves to be studied, taken as a model, and put into practice! In response to your illuminating question, I venture to present its broad outline. The Rites of Zhou is a sage’s book for ordering the world. The Duke of Zhou took the substance of fully realized human relationships and made it function through a comprehensive system of institutions; grounded in the learning of inner sagehood, he established the standards of outward kingship. From the Yellow Emperor down through the two dynasties, he followed what was appropriate to the prevailing influences and conditions, responded to changes in the times and circumstances, and judiciously made reductions and additions. Thus he brought together the achievements of the many sages and established the settled institutions of a king. Consider how the opening of each section says: “The king establishes the capital and distinguishes…”

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
方正位體國經野設官分職以爲民極則
其非止治岐之政理財之書可見矣故其
旨遠其事密其義該尚而當盡而不迂上
而天地日月如土均土圭之法下而封域
山川若封人虔衙之制著而禮樂刑政若
肆師大司樂土師之掌微而禽獸草木若
内饔甸師鼈人食醫之事纖悉備具蓋誠
有以極規模之大盡節目之詳建天地質
鬼神已驗於當時而不利於來世者也漢
===
唐以來雖未能悉遵古制而官聯服御車
旗禮儀之節率有取焉猶爲圓之不能踰
規方之不能外矩者亦可以見是書之可
尊與其法之可行也斷然矣夫何秦火之
餘此書晚出巖壁河間獻王得而上之又
取考工記以補冬官之闕故武帝因謂末
世瀆亂之書成帝時劉歆校理秘書識其
可用遂輔新室以泉府理財之說故漢儒
始有六國陰謀之訾歆不足責也至於鄭
punctuated:
方，正位，體國經野，設官分職，以爲民極」，則其非止治岐之政、理財之書可見矣。故其旨遠，其事密，其義該，尚而當，盡而不迂。上而天地日月，如土均土圭之法；下而封域山川，若封人虔衙之制；著而禮樂刑政，若肆師、大司樂、土師之掌；微而禽獸草木，若内饔、甸師、鼈人、食醫之事，纖悉備具。蓋誠有以極規模之大，盡節目之詳，建天地，質鬼神，已驗於當時而不利於來世者也。漢唐以來，雖未能悉遵古制，而官聯、服御、車旗、禮儀之節，率有取焉，猶爲圓之不能踰規，方之不能外矩者，亦可以見是書之可尊與其法之可行也，斷然矣。
夫何秦火之餘，此書晚出巖壁，河間獻王得而上之，又取考工記以補冬官之闕，故武帝因謂末世瀆亂之書。成帝時，劉歆校理秘書，識其可用，遂輔新室以泉府理財之說，故漢儒始有六國陰謀之訾。歆不足責也，至於鄭
translation_en:
…the orientations, rectifies positions, lays out the capital and demarcates the countryside, establishes offices and assigns duties, thereby setting a standard for the people.” Thus it is clear that this is not merely a record of government at Qi or a book on managing finances. Its purport is far-reaching, its provisions meticulous, and its meaning comprehensive: elevated yet appropriate, exhaustive yet not impractical. Above, it addresses heaven and earth, sun and moon, through such methods as land equalization and the use of the earthen gnomon; below, it addresses territorial boundaries, mountains, and rivers, through such institutions as the Boundary Officer and “Qianya” [?]. In manifest matters, it addresses rites, music, punishments, and government through the responsibilities of the Assistant Grand Master of Ceremonies, the Music Master-in-chief, and the Judicial Officer [?]; in minute matters, it addresses birds, beasts, plants, and trees through the duties of the Inner Cook, the Officer of the Royal Fields, the Turtle Catcher, and the Dietitian. Every fine detail is provided for. Truly, it encompasses the greatest scope and exhausts the particulars of every provision. It can be established before heaven and earth and tested before ghosts and spirits; it was proven in its own time, yet is not beneficial to later ages [?]. Since the Han and Tang, although it has not been possible to follow all the ancient institutions, arrangements for coordinating offices, imperial dress and equipment, carriages and banners, and ceremonial observances have generally drawn upon it. Just as one cannot draw a circle beyond the compass or a square outside the carpenter’s square, this shows conclusively that the book deserves reverence and that its methods can be put into practice.
How, then, did matters come to this? After the Qin book-burning, this book emerged late from a rocky wall. Prince Xian of Hejian obtained it and presented it to the throne, also taking the Record of Artificers (Kaogong ji) to fill the missing section on the Winter Offices. Emperor Wu consequently called it a book of the corruption and disorder of a declining age. During Emperor Cheng’s reign, Liu Xin collated the books in the palace collection and recognized that it could be used. He subsequently assisted the Xin dynasty with its teachings on financial administration through the Treasury Office. Thus Han scholars began to disparage it as a work of secret schemes from the Six States. Xin is hardly worth reproaching. As for Zheng…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
玄析袁劉杜二鄭爲之註疏然一引緯書
訛於天帝之異名二引司馬法誤以丘乘
爲丘甸三引春秋傳謂王服止於九章四
引左傳國語謂我周之有分野五引漢儒
禮記則以夫人而亂王后副褘之飾此其
失也然此皆其小者也一節可疑不害於
全體之可信冬官雖缺而五官固在也考
工記特任萬民之一職宜不足以厭學者
之心而籍其口吳澄謂冡未嘗亡雜於五
===
官之中者未爲無據至於三易則大卜筮
人之守四詩則大師籥章之司尚書爲外
史之職春秋亦太史之事總其全書當必
包括五經蓋不特相爲表裏者而其精華
純粹固已見取夫子久矣是其大者之必
可信如此故唐書謂其義可幽贊神明文
可經緯邦國程子謂周禮一書須知道者
觀之可決是非而朱子亦謂其間細碎處
雖可疑其大體直是非聖人不能作故愚
punctuated: 玄析袁、劉、杜、二鄭，爲之註疏。然一引緯書，訛於天帝之異名；二引司馬法，誤以丘乘爲丘甸；三引春秋傳，謂王服止於九章；四引左傳、國語，謂我周之有分野；五引漢儒禮記，則以夫人而亂王后副褘之飾。此其失也。然此皆其小者也，一節可疑，不害於全體之可信。冬官雖缺，而五官固在也。考工記特任萬民之一職，宜不足以厭學者之心而籍其口。吳澄謂冡未嘗亡，雜於五官之中者，未爲無據。至於三易，則大卜、筮人之守；四詩，則大師、籥章之司；尚書爲外史之職，春秋亦太史之事。總其全書，當必包括五經，蓋不特相爲表裏者，而其精華純粹，固已見取夫子久矣。是其大者之必可信如此。故唐書謂其義可幽贊神明，文可經緯邦國。程子謂周禮一書，須知道者觀之，可決是非；而朱子亦謂其間細碎處雖可疑，其大體直是非聖人不能作。故愚
translation_en:
…Xuan analyzed the interpretations of Yuan, Liu, Du, and the two Zhengs [?] and supplied commentaries and subcommentaries on it. Yet, first, he cited the apocryphal writings and erred concerning the different names of Heaven and the Supreme Sovereign. Second, he cited the Methods of the Marshal (Sima fa) and mistakenly treated qiu and sheng as qiu and dian, units of territorial organization. Third, he cited the Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals and maintained that the king’s robes bore only nine emblems. Fourth, he cited the Zuo Commentary and the Discourses of the States to assert that our Zhou dynasty had terrestrial regions assigned to celestial divisions. Fifth, he cited the Han scholars’ Record of Rites, thereby confusing the ornaments of noble consorts with the queen’s ceremonial headdress and pheasant-patterned robe. These were his errors. Yet these are all minor matters: doubt about one passage does not impair the credibility of the whole. Although the Offices of Winter is missing, the other five offices certainly remain. The Record of Crafts concerns only one of the occupations assigned to the common people; naturally, it cannot satisfy scholars’ minds and silence their objections. Wu Cheng’s claim that the Offices of Winter [?] was never lost, but is interspersed among the other five offices, is not without foundation.

As for the three Changes, these were in the keeping of the Grand Diviner and the milfoil diviners; the four divisions of the Odes were under the charge of the Grand Music Master and the officials responsible for flute music. The Book of Documents fell within the duties of the Outer Scribe, and the Spring and Autumn Annals likewise belonged to the work of the Grand Scribe. Taken as a whole, the book must encompass the Five Classics. Indeed, it does more than complement them: its finest and purest substance had already been adopted by the Master long ago. Such is the assured credibility of its major principles. Thus the History of the Tang says that its meaning can mysteriously assist the spirits, and its text can give structure and order to the realm. Master Cheng said that the Rites of Zhou must be read by someone who understands the Way, who can then judge what is right and wrong. Master Zhu likewise said that although some minute details may be doubtful, its overall structure is truly something that none but a sage could have created. Therefore, I, in my humble view…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
謂或闕之以俟知或補之以就正但信其
大而不屑屑於其小者亦庶乎可以尊先
聖之經矣至若元魏北齊以來授田分鄉
者蓋十用其一二蘇綽在周約六典以建
官府兵之制微有端緒亦十用其五六隋
文帝之富盛蘇威文景之損益亦既十用
其七八矣而治不古若者蓋竊聖人之似
而不得其真況皆舉一而廢百得此而失
彼夫王道如精金美玉豈容雜也雜則敗
===
矣故曰假而用之者莽也輕而用之者綽
也誤而用之者安石也而蘇子所謂大用
則王小用則亡者也若數人者蓋知王道
而小用之也豈周禮之罪哉至唐太宗則
尤可怪者觀夫貞觀之治世業以授田租
庸調以取民七百三十員以建官十六衛
八百府以置兵雖於周禮多所模倣至其
言曰周禮真聖作也不井田不封建不肉
刑欲行周公之道不可得也夫太宗居可
punctuated: 謂或闕之以俟知，或補之以就正，但信其大而不屑屑於其小者，亦庶乎可以尊先聖之經矣。至若元魏、北齊以來授田分鄉者，蓋十用其一二；蘇綽在周，約六典以建官，府兵之制微有端緒，亦十用其五六；隋文帝之富盛，蘇威文景之損益，亦既十用其七八矣。而治不古若者，蓋竊聖人之似而不得其真，況皆舉一而廢百，得此而失彼。夫王道如精金美玉，豈容雜也？雜則敗矣。故曰：「假而用之者，莽也；輕而用之者，綽也；誤而用之者，安石也。」而蘇子所謂「大用則王，小用則亡」者也。若數人者，蓋知王道而小用之也，豈周禮之罪哉？至唐太宗，則尤可怪者。觀夫貞觀之治，世業以授田，租庸調以取民，七百三十員以建官，十六衛八百府以置兵，雖於周禮多所模倣，至其言曰：「周禮真聖作也。不井田，不封建，不肉刑，欲行周公之道，不可得也。」夫太宗居可
translation_en:
…I therefore say that, whether one leaves gaps pending fuller understanding or supplies omissions to arrive at a correct text, if one trusts its broad principles without fussing over its minor details, one may perhaps duly honor the classic of the former sage. As for the allocation of land and division into townships from the Northern Wei and Northern Qi onward, these employed perhaps one or two tenths of it. Under the Northern Zhou, Su Chuo drew upon the Six Statutes to establish offices, and the militia system began to take shape: this too employed five or six tenths of it. With the wealth and prosperity under Emperor Wen of the Sui, and the adjustments of Su Wei and Wen Jing [?], seven or eight tenths of it had already been employed. Yet their government fell short of antiquity because they appropriated a semblance of the sage’s institutions without attaining their true substance. Moreover, they all adopted one measure while abandoning a hundred others, gaining this while losing that. The kingly Way is like refined gold or fine jade: how could it admit adulteration? Adulterate it, and it is ruined.
Thus it is said: “Wang Mang employed it disingenuously; Su Chuo employed it lightly; Wang Anshi employed it mistakenly.” This is what Master Su meant by “Employ it fully, and one becomes a true king; employ it partially, and one perishes.” These men understood the kingly Way but employed it only partially. How could this be the fault of the Rites of Zhou?
As for Emperor Taizong of the Tang, his case is particularly puzzling. Consider the government of the Zhenguan reign: land was allocated as hereditary holdings; grain tax, labor service, and textile levies were exacted from the people; 730 officials were appointed to establish the administration; and sixteen Guards and eight hundred military headquarters were established to organize the troops. Although he modeled many things on the Rites of Zhou, he nevertheless said: “The Rites of Zhou truly is the work of a sage. Without the well-field system, the enfeoffment system, and mutilating punishments, it is impossible to put the Duke of Zhou’s Way into practice.” Now Taizong occupied a position in which he could…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
致之位又當開創之初使其悉意經理以
爲民極何不可者顧乃付之浩歎而不盡
用豈非悅而不繹雜而無本故邪其漸不
克終有自矣然此皆其迹也師迹而無實
不若師意而可行今夫立於百世之上以
俟乎百世之下者聖人之心也奮乎百世
之下而考諸百世之上者吾人之志也有
時焉不能以皆合勢焉不可以强同令之
不可爲古猶古之不可以爲今也聖人且
===
柰何哉於此不師其意可乎夫冢宰總六
典佐王均邦國者今冢宰固設也唯其能
一天下之政已矣五官各一職佐王治邦
國者今五官固設也唯其能理庶官之政
已矣每鄉六十屬今六鄉之屬固不止三
百六十也可以意汰之乎井牧之法難行
矣授田限田以養民其可乎鄉三物之法
不行矣學校賓興將大比其德行可乎爵
秩固懸也而無封疆朝覲固舉也而無聘
punctuated: 致之位，又當開創之初，使其悉意經理，以爲民極，何不可者？顧乃付之浩歎而不盡用，豈非悅而不繹、雜而無本故邪？其漸不克終有自矣。然此皆其迹也，師迹而無實，不若師意而可行。今夫立於百世之上，以俟乎百世之下者，聖人之心也；奮乎百世之下，而考諸百世之上者，吾人之志也。有時焉不能以皆合，勢焉不可以强同，令之不可爲古，猶古之不可以爲今也。聖人且柰何哉？於此不師其意可乎？夫冢宰總六典，佐王均邦國者，今冢宰固設也，唯其能一天下之政已矣。五官各一職，佐王治邦國者，今五官固設也，唯其能理庶官之政已矣。每鄉六十屬，今六鄉之屬固不止三百六十也，可以意汰之乎？井牧之法難行矣，授田限田以養民，其可乎？鄉三物之法不行矣，學校賓興，將大比其德行，可乎？爵秩固懸也，而無封疆；朝覲固舉也，而無聘
translation_en:
…a position from which he could accomplish this, and moreover stood at the beginning of a dynasty. Had he devoted his whole mind to ordering its affairs and becoming a model for the people, what could he not have done? Instead, he left the matter to deep sighs and failed to put it fully into practice. Was this not because he delighted in it without pursuing its implications, mixing different approaches without a firm foundation? His gradual failure to carry through to the end thus had its source.

Yet all these are merely outward precedents. To imitate precedents without their substance is inferior to following their underlying intent in ways that can be put into practice. To stand a hundred generations before and await those a hundred generations afterward: this is the mind of the sage. To exert ourselves a hundred generations afterward and examine what came a hundred generations before: this is our aspiration. There are differences of time that cannot all be reconciled, and circumstances that cannot forcibly be made identical. The present cannot be made into antiquity [?], just as antiquity cannot be made into the present. What could even a sage do about this? In such circumstances, can we fail to follow the underlying intent?

The Minister of State oversaw the six administrative codes and assisted the king in bringing the states into balance. Today, the office of Minister of State is indeed established; what matters is simply that he can unify the administration of the realm. The five ministers each had their own charge and assisted the king in governing the states. Today, these five ministries are indeed established; what matters is simply that they can order the administration of the various officials. Each district had sixty subordinate units. Today, the subordinate units of the six districts certainly number more than three hundred and sixty. Could they be reduced in accordance with the underlying intent? The well-field system of allotting arable and pastoral land is difficult to implement. Might granting land and limiting landholdings serve to sustain the people? The district system of instruction in the three categories is no longer practiced. Might schools and the ceremonial honoring and recommendation of worthy men provide for a great triennial assessment of their virtue and conduct? Ranks and grades are indeed established, but without territorial fiefs; court audiences are indeed held, but without diplomatic visits…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
問所以酌今之宜而不失古之意者可講
也又其大者如比閭族黨州鄉之民即所
以爲伍兩卒旅師軍之衆此則周家致太
平之基也今以其意而容民畜衆可乎冢
宰制王之左右自飲食衣服侍從之類無
不禀命焉此又所以防君側之惡而謹其
心術之微也今欲使之出入起居有不
臧左右前後無非正人豈無可義起之法
乎凡此皆其意之可師者也孔子所謂殷
===
因於夏禮周因於殷禮所損益可知者今
將損益周禮而用之可不可也昔者周公
兼三王以施四事其有不合者仰思繼日
安知周禮所載非其得之待旦者乎設今
周公可復作焉其所以仰思待旦不知又
何如也故愚以爲或酌之以今或通之
而宜俗直師其意而不拘拘於其迹者亦
庶乎可以遵先王之法矣雖然意固師古
之方心實行法之本故不忍人之政由於
punctuated: 問。所以酌今之宜而不失古之意者，可講也。又其大者，如比閭族黨州鄉之民，即所以爲伍兩卒旅師軍之衆，此則周家致太平之基也。今以其意而容民畜衆，可乎？冢宰制王之左右，自飲食衣服侍從之類，無不禀命焉。此又所以防君側之惡，而謹其心術之微也。今欲使之出入起居有不臧，左右前後無非正人，豈無可義起之法乎？凡此皆其意之可師者也。孔子所謂「殷因於夏禮，周因於殷禮，所損益可知」者，今將損益周禮而用之，可不可也？昔者周公兼三王以施四事，其有不合者，仰思繼日，安知周禮所載非其得之待旦者乎？設今周公可復作焉，其所以仰思待旦，不知又何如也。故愚以爲，或酌之以今，或通之而宜俗，直師其意而不拘拘於其迹者，亦庶乎可以遵先王之法矣。雖然，意固師古之方，心實行法之本。故不忍人之政由於
translation_en:
…ceremonial inquiries. How to weigh what is appropriate today without losing the intent of antiquity is something we can discuss. Consider also a matter of greater importance: the people organized into neighborhood groups, hamlets, clans, communities, districts, and townships were the very people who constituted the military squads, platoons, companies, battalions, regiments, and armies. This was the foundation on which the Zhou house achieved Great Peace. Could we now follow its intent to accommodate the people and nurture the multitude? The Minister of State regulated those around the king: all those responsible for his food, clothing, and personal attendance received their orders from him. This, too, served to guard against evil at the ruler’s side and to exercise care over the subtlest workings of his mind. If today we wished to ensure that there was something improper in his movements and daily conduct [?], and that everyone to his left and right, before and behind him, was an upright person, could there be no measures devised in accordance with righteousness? In all these matters, the underlying intent offers a model to follow. Confucius said, “Yin followed the rites of Xia; Zhou followed the rites of Yin; what they subtracted and added can be known.” Could we now likewise subtract from and add to the Rites of Zhou and put them into practice?

In former times, the Duke of Zhou drew together the ways of the Three Kings to carry out four undertakings. Wherever these did not accord, he looked upward in thought, continuing through the day. How do we know that what is recorded in the Rites of Zhou was not what he arrived at while awaiting dawn? Suppose the Duke of Zhou could rise again today: who knows what thoughts would occupy him as he looked upward and awaited dawn? Thus, in my humble opinion, if we weigh these institutions against present circumstances, or adapt them to suit prevailing customs, taking their intent as our model without clinging rigidly to their outward forms, we may come close to following the laws of the former kings. Nevertheless, although grasping their intent is indeed the way to emulate antiquity, the heart is truly the foundation for putting laws into practice. Thus, government that cannot bear the suffering of others arises from…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
不忍人之心非有關雎麟趾之意則不可
以行周官之法度我
國家深仁厚澤重熈累洽百五六十年于玆
正薰蒸融液積德可興之時也昔
太祖稽古建官悉依六典是其大者固已尊信
篤行特未盡而若有待焉耳恭惟
皇上神聖中興孜孜化理而群賢一德恊和賛
襄斯所謂人存政舉者倘以是書列之
經筵措諸典禮則成周之治復見今日此千
===
載一時也草茅雖賤豈無王仲淹之志惟
與其進尚當有以
獻焉
第五問
畢鸞杰笈
同考試官教諭陳 批〔變異之理不明止以諸儒之說不定則省脩之道亦無所主子能折衷諸說之得失而〕
〔以正心格天爲本斷制精當深切〕
聖心變非言語文字之學所可及者
punctuated:
不忍人之心。非有關雎麟趾之意，則不可以行周官之法度。我國家深仁厚澤，重熈累洽，百五六十年于玆，正薰蒸融液、積德可興之時也。昔太祖稽古建官，悉依六典，是其大者固已尊信篤行，特未盡而若有待焉耳。恭惟皇上神聖中興，孜孜化理，而群賢一德恊和賛襄，斯所謂人存政舉者。倘以是書列之經筵，措諸典禮，則成周之治復見今日，此千載一時也。草茅雖賤，豈無王仲淹之志？惟與其進，尚當有以獻焉。

第五問

畢鸞杰笈

同考試官教諭陳批〔變異之理不明，止以諸儒之說不定，則省脩之道亦無所主。子能折衷諸說之得失，而〕〔以正心格天爲本，斷制精當，深切〕聖心，變非言語文字之學所可及者。
translation_en:
…a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others. Without the spirit of “Guanju” (The Ospreys) and “Linzhi” (The Qilin’s Hoof), one cannot put into practice the regulations of the Offices of Zhou. Our dynasty’s profound benevolence and abundant bounty, its successive ages of brilliance and accumulated peace, have now endured for a hundred and fifty or sixty years. This is precisely the time when their pervasive, transforming influence and accumulated virtue can bring about a flourishing age. Formerly, Taizu consulted antiquity in establishing offices, following throughout the six codes of administration. In its major principles, he already revered and trusted this work and earnestly put it into practice; only its implementation remained incomplete, as though awaiting a later occasion. We reverently reflect that His Majesty, in his inspired sagacity, has brought about a restoration and labors tirelessly at moral transformation and good government, while the assembled worthies, united in purpose, harmoniously assist him. This is what is meant by “when the right men are present, their government flourishes.” If this book were included in the Classics Colloquium and its principles embodied in institutional rites, the government of the perfected Zhou would appear again today. This is an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years. Though a humble man of the countryside, could I be without the aspirations of Wang Zhongyan? If only my advancement were encouraged, I should yet have something to offer.

Fifth Question

Bi Luan (畢鸞); the following characters, 杰笈, are unclear [?].

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: 〔The principles underlying anomalies are not understood simply because the explanations of the various Confucian scholars remain unsettled; consequently, the way of self-examination and self-cultivation also lacks a guiding principle. You are able to weigh the merits and shortcomings of the various explanations and〕〔take rectifying the mind and reaching Heaven as your foundation. Your judgments are precise and appropriate, profoundly touching〕 the imperial mind. This is beyond the reach of mere learning in words and literary composition [the character 變 here is doubtful].

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
〔考試官教授吳　批〕〔論災異所以成就〕
聖明之德善推天心仁愛之意末以聖人無災異而亦懼則聖賢傳心要法正在
于此子能言之其必究天人之學而得其門者矣
考試官教授王　批〔論天人相與之際精切允當〕
且忠蓋之意溢於言外非深達政體者固未易到也有士
如此可以爲矣
上天垂戒之意徵于變人君弭變之實存
乎德災異之來固所以成人君之德也脩
德以消變則人事備而天道順仁愛之意
===
寓于拂逆之中無言之妙亦惟應之以心
而已是其休祥滋至所以益吾之過而災
異疊興者適所以增吾之不能豈可以常
數自諉而忘其恐懼之念哉執事發策以
災異爲問蓋有切於當時之急務仰見我
皇上憂勤之心而欲爲
聖德之裨也嘗聞天人一理感應一機沖漠之
際相爲流通自夫拟與之說行而後天人
之理背甘石之言出而後感應之機誣矣
punctuated:
〔考試官教授吳　批〕〔論災異所以成就〕聖明之德，善推天心仁愛之意。末以聖人無災異而亦懼，則聖賢傳心要法正在于此。子能言之，其必究天人之學而得其門者矣。
考試官教授王　批〔論天人相與之際精切允當〕且忠蓋之意溢於言外，非深達政體者固未易到也。有士如此，可以爲矣。
上天垂戒之意徵于變，人君弭變之實存乎德。災異之來，固所以成人君之德也。脩德以消變，則人事備而天道順。仁愛之意寓于拂逆之中，無言之妙亦惟應之以心而已。是其休祥滋至，所以益吾之過，而災異疊興者，適所以增吾之不能，豈可以常數自諉而忘其恐懼之念哉？執事發策以災異爲問，蓋有切於當時之急務，仰見我皇上憂勤之心，而欲爲聖德之裨也。嘗聞天人一理，感應一機，沖漠之際，相爲流通。自夫拟與之說行，而後天人之理背；甘石之言出，而後感應之機誣矣。
translation_en:
〔Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor:〕〔The discussion of how calamities and anomalies perfect〕 the virtue of the sagely and enlightened ruler ably elucidates Heaven’s benevolent and loving intent. At the end, the statement that sages remain fearful even without calamities and anomalies identifies precisely the essential method by which sages and worthies transmit their understanding of the mind. Since you can articulate this, you must have investigated the learning concerning Heaven and humanity and found its entrance.
