title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
無欲速無見小利欲速則不達見小利則
大事不成
陳德文
同考試官教諭馬　批　〔題本簡易明白作者詞多重複此篇數言即了其義校之以政必能達者〕
同考試官教諭黃　批　〔聖人告子夏之言正爲政者所當戒此作得之〕
同考試官教諭潘　批　〔隱括政體得夫子言外之意〕
考試官教授吳　批　〔辭不繁而意自足錄之〕
考試官教授王　批　〔遲速小大之間王伯之所由分也夫子雖未明言而意已寓子能發之可以占爲政矣〕
===
聖人告賢者爲政當戒夫近小而必申言其弊
焉蓋爲政當以遠大爲期也苟務近小則各有
其弊矣可不以是爲戒哉子夏問政聖人告之
意謂爲政之道遲速之間而通塞攸係大小之
判而成不成所關子之宰莒父也可不審其初
punctuated:
第壹場
四書
「無欲速，無見小利。欲速則不達，見小利則大事不成。」
陳德文
同考試官教諭馬批〔題本簡易明白，作者詞多重複。此篇數言即了其義，校之以政，必能達者。〕
同考試官教諭黃批〔聖人告子夏之言，正爲政者所當戒，此作得之。〕
同考試官教諭潘批〔隱括政體，得夫子言外之意。〕
考試官教授吳批〔辭不繁而意自足，錄之。〕
考試官教授王批〔遲速小大之間，王伯之所由分也。夫子雖未明言，而意已寓。子能發之，可以占爲政矣。〕
聖人告賢者爲政，當戒夫近小，而必申言其弊焉。蓋爲政當以遠大爲期也，苟務近小，則各有其弊矣，可不以是爲戒哉？子夏問政，聖人告之，意謂爲政之道，遲速之間而通塞攸係，大小之判而成不成所關。子之宰莒父也，可不審其初
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“Do not desire haste; do not look to small gains. Desiring haste prevents attainment; looking to small gains prevents great undertakings from succeeding.”
Chen Dewen

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Instructor: 〔The topic is inherently simple and clear, yet writers often repeat themselves. This essay explains its meaning in just a few words. Judged in relation to government, its author would surely be capable of attaining his aims.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: 〔The sage’s words to Zixia concern precisely what those who govern should guard against. This composition grasps their meaning.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor: 〔It encapsulates the essentials of government and grasps what the Master meant beyond his explicit words.〕

Comment by Examiner Wu, Professor: 〔Its language is concise, yet its meaning is complete. Include it.〕

Comment by Examiner Wang, Professor: 〔The distinction between slowness and haste, between small and great, is the basis for the division between kingly and hegemonic rule. Although the Master did not state this explicitly, the meaning is already implicit. Your ability to bring it out allows us to judge your capacity to govern.〕

The sage told a worthy man that, in governing, he must guard against pursuing immediate results and small gains, and necessarily elaborated on their harmful consequences. For government should aim at what is far-reaching and great. If one pursues immediate results and small gains, each brings its own harm. Can one fail to take warning from this? When Zixia asked about government, the sage’s reply meant that, in the way of governing, the distinction between slowness and haste determines whether progress is open or obstructed, and the distinction between great and small bears upon success or failure. As you govern Jufu, can you fail to examine carefully at the outset…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
其贊矣非天下之至誠其孰能有之而非天下
之至聖其孰知之哉抑論上言至聖之德分其
屬而言也所以爲小德之川流也此言至誠之
道合其本而言也所以爲大德之敦化也其實
一也所以皆天道也由是觀之君子之學析之
不可以不精而合之不可以不大析之精則爲
其大者益力合之大則爲其精者益盡其要在
於誠之而已
滄浪之水清兮可以濯我纓滄浪之水濁
===
兮可以濯我足孔子曰小子聽之清斯
濯纓濁斯濯足矣自取之也
周麟
同考試官訓導吴　批　〔古有滄浪之歌孺子偶述而歌之耳非歌於滄浪之上也作者尋源遡流恐失本旨此〕
同考試官訓導張　批　〔篇斟量重輕詞通意暢講後數語讀之令人灑然講自取處甚明快可錄〕
考試官教授吴　批　〔題本枯淡而意在言外此作詞能達意且宛轉含蓄聽者不覺凋人刻之〕
punctuated:
其贊矣。非天下之至誠，其孰能有之？而非天下之至聖，其孰知之哉？抑論上言至聖之德，分其屬而言也，所以爲小德之川流也；此言至誠之道，合其本而言也，所以爲大德之敦化也。其實一也，所以皆天道也。由是觀之，君子之學，析之不可以不精，而合之不可以不大。析之精，則爲其大者益力；合之大，則爲其精者益盡。其要在於誠之而已。

「滄浪之水清兮，可以濯我纓；滄浪之水濁兮，可以濯我足。」孔子曰：「小子聽之！清斯濯纓，濁斯濯足矣，自取之也。」

周麟

同考試官訓導吴，批：〔古有滄浪之歌，孺子偶述而歌之耳，非歌於滄浪之上也。作者尋源遡流，恐失本旨。此〕

同考試官訓導張，批：〔篇斟量重輕，詞通意暢。講後數語，讀之令人灑然。講自取處甚明快，可錄。〕

考試官教授吴，批：〔題本枯淡，而意在言外。此作詞能達意，且宛轉含蓄，聽者不覺凋人，刻之。〕
translation_en:
…its assistance. Unless one possessed the utmost sincerity under Heaven, who could possess this? And unless one possessed the utmost sageliness under Heaven, who could understand it? Moreover, the preceding discussion of the virtue of utmost sageliness speaks of its attributes separately: this is why the lesser virtues are like flowing streams. Here, the discussion of the Way of utmost sincerity speaks of these together in their common root: this is why the greater virtue brings about profound transformation. In substance they are one, and thus both are the Way of Heaven. Viewed in this light, the gentleman’s learning must be precise in its analysis and comprehensive in its synthesis. Precision in analysis strengthens his efforts toward comprehensiveness; comprehensiveness in synthesis makes his pursuit of precision still more thorough. The essential point lies simply in making oneself sincere.

“When the waters of the Canglang are clear, I can wash my cap strings in them; when the waters of the Canglang are muddy, I can wash my feet in them.” Confucius said: “My young disciples, listen! When clear, they are used to wash cap strings; when muddy, they are used to wash feet. They bring this treatment upon themselves.”

Zhou Lin.

Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor, comments: “There was an ancient Song of the Canglang; the boy merely happened to recite and sing it. He was not singing on the banks of the Canglang. In seeking the source and tracing the current upstream, the author may have missed the original purport. This …”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “…piece weighs the relative importance of its points; its language flows and its meaning comes through freely. Reading the exposition of the final few phrases leaves one refreshed. Its explanation of ‘bringing this upon oneself’ is especially clear and incisive. Worth including.”

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The topic is inherently dry and plain, but its meaning lies beyond the words. The language of this composition conveys that meaning, while remaining subtle and suggestive. Those who hear it are unaware of its ‘withering people’ [?]. Have it engraved for printing.”

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授王　批〔發明孟子戒當時之意令人〕
警省
大賢述孺子詠物以適其情聖人聞言而發其
理其警當時之意深矣蓋事變未有無故而至
者也即聖人有取於孺子之歌則不仁之禍夫
豈由於人哉昔孟子論不仁之不可與言至此
蓋謂禍福無自來之理在人有感召之幾獨不
觀孺子之歌與孔子之言乎彼孺子之歌曰滄
浪之水有清者焉本源未撓而靜深澄徹則可
===
就之而濯我之纓滌舊染而爲新渾然物我之
一體也滄浪之水有濁者焉蒙泉已汩而沸潰
溷淆則可以之而濯我之足去積汙而自潔悠
然內外之兩忘也孺子因物感興於順適之餘
聖人聲入心通於言意之表乃呼門人而謂之
曰至理不遺於小物恒情多忽於適言孺子之
歌小子其聽之哉夫惟水之清而不可以輕用
也斯以之而濯纓夫惟水之濁而不可以遂棄
也斯以之而濯足以水之清而自得乎濯之貴
punctuated:
考試官教授王批〔發明孟子戒當時之意，令人〕警省。

大賢述孺子詠物以適其情，聖人聞言而發其理，其警當時之意深矣。蓋事變未有無故而至者也。即聖人有取於孺子之歌，則不仁之禍，夫豈由於人哉？昔孟子論不仁之不可與言，至此蓋謂禍福無自來之理，在人有感召之幾。獨不觀孺子之歌與孔子之言乎？彼孺子之歌曰：「滄浪之水有清者焉，本源未撓而靜深澄徹，則可就之而濯我之纓，滌舊染而爲新，渾然物我之一體也。滄浪之水有濁者焉，蒙泉已汩而沸潰溷淆，則可以之而濯我之足，去積汙而自潔，悠然內外之兩忘也。」孺子因物感興於順適之餘，聖人聲入心通於言意之表，乃呼門人而謂之曰：「至理不遺於小物，恒情多忽於適言。孺子之歌，小子其聽之哉！夫惟水之清而不可以輕用也，斯以之而濯纓；夫惟水之濁而不可以遂棄也，斯以之而濯足。以水之清而自得乎濯之貴，
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Wang, an Instructor: 〔“It elucidates Mencius’s intention to admonish the people of his time, prompting readers〕 to vigilance and reflection.”

The great worthy recounts how a child sang of things to give expression to his feelings, and how the sage, hearing his words, brought out their underlying principle. Profound indeed was his intention to admonish the people of his time. Changes in affairs never occur without a cause. Given that even the sage found something worth drawing upon in the child’s song, how could the calamities of inhumanity originate with other people? When Mencius, discussing why one cannot reason with the inhumane, reached this point, his meaning was that neither calamity nor good fortune comes of itself: the incipient causes that summon them lie in people themselves. Have we not considered the child’s song and Confucius’s words?

The child’s song says: “There are times when the waters of the Canglang are clear. Their source undisturbed, they are still, deep, and limpid; then I can go to them and wash my cap strings, cleansing away old stains and making them new. Things and self form one seamless whole. There are times when the waters of the Canglang are muddy. The spring waters have been churned up, surging, spilling, and mingling in turbidity; then I can use them to wash my feet, removing accumulated dirt and cleansing myself. At ease, I forget both what is within and what is without.”

Inspired by what he encountered, the child gave voice to his feelings in a moment of ease and contentment. As the sound entered the sage’s ears, his mind grasped what lay beyond the words and their expressed meaning. He therefore called his disciples and said: “The ultimate principle is not absent even from small things, yet ordinary people often overlook it in casual utterances. My young disciples, listen to the child’s song! Precisely because the water is clear and should not be used carelessly, one uses it to wash cap strings. Precisely because the water is muddy yet should not simply be discarded, one uses it to wash one’s feet. Through its clarity, the water of itself obtains the more honored use in washing …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
初無心於纓也亦無心於水也物理之相符若
有推之而不得者矣使有時而濁焉安知不以
之而濯足乎以水之濁而自得乎濯之賤初何
心於水也亦何心於足也氣類之相應若有避
之而不能者矣使有時而清焉安知不以之而
濯纓乎夫此一滄浪也唯其有清濁之殊是以
有致用之異人非不仁禍亦何由而至哉大抵
禍固以不仁而致也有能去不仁而求仁亦可
以轉其禍而爲福太甲之興也以桐秦穆之防
===
也以殽檇李勝吳會稽强越其明驗也戰國之
君私欲蔽固皆不能去禍以求福其終於敗亡
也固宜孔孟自取之言其亦重有感也夫
易
貞固足以幹事
歐陽塾
同考試官教諭馬 批〔他卷講貞固幹事處語多支複是篇說理詳明措詞簡當錄之以式多士〕
同考試官教諭黃 批〔幹事處體認明白足可以語〕
punctuated:
初無心於纓也，亦無心於水也。物理之相符，若有推之而不得者矣。使有時而濁焉，安知不以之而濯足乎？以水之濁而自得乎濯之賤，初何心於水也，亦何心於足也？氣類之相應，若有避之而不能者矣。使有時而清焉，安知不以之而濯纓乎？夫此一滄浪也，唯其有清濁之殊，是以有致用之異。人非不仁，禍亦何由而至哉？大抵禍固以不仁而致也，有能去不仁而求仁，亦可以轉其禍而爲福。太甲之興也以桐，秦穆之防也以殽，檇李勝吳，會稽强越，其明驗也。戰國之君，私欲蔽固，皆不能去禍以求福，其終於敗亡也固宜。孔孟自取之言，其亦重有感也夫！

易
貞固足以幹事。
歐陽塾

同考試官教諭馬批〔他卷講貞固幹事處，語多支複。是篇說理詳明，措詞簡當，錄之以式多士。〕

同考試官教諭黃批〔幹事處體認明白，足可以語〕
translation_en:
…There was originally no deliberate concern for the cap strings, nor any deliberate concern for the water. The correspondence between the principles inherent in things seems impossible to reject. If the water should at some time become muddy, how do we know it would not be used to wash one's feet? When muddy water finds its fitting use in the lowly task of washing, what deliberate concern was there originally for the water, or for the feet? The mutual response of things of kindred vital force seems impossible to evade. If the water should at some time become clear, how do we know it would not be used to wash one's cap strings? This is the same Canglang River: only because its water differs in clarity and muddiness does its application differ. If a person were not inhumane, by what means could calamity come upon him? In general, calamity is indeed brought about by inhumanity. If one can abandon inhumanity and seek humaneness, one can also turn calamity into good fortune. Tai Jia's resurgence came through his stay at Tong; Duke Mu of Qin's vigilance [?] came through Xiao. At Zuili, Wu was defeated; at Kuaiji, Yue was strengthened. These are clear proofs. The rulers of the Warring States were blinded and entrenched in their selfish desires; none could avert calamity and seek good fortune. It was only fitting that they should ultimately meet defeat and destruction. Surely Confucius and Mencius, in speaking of what people bring upon themselves, were expressing deeply felt concerns!

Book of Changes
“Being steadfast and firm is sufficient to manage affairs.”
Ouyang Shu

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Instructor: 〔In other papers, the discussion of steadfastness, firmness, and managing affairs is often rambling and repetitive. This essay explains the principles thoroughly and clearly, with concise and apt wording. It is selected to serve as a model for the many candidates.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor: 〔The discussion of managing affairs shows clear understanding, sufficient to qualify the author to discuss …〕

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
易矣
同考試官教諭潘　批〔易義類能言之求其粹淨精〕〔微者無踰此篇〕
考試官教授吳　批〔非精于易者不能故錄〕
考試官教授王　批〔得文言之旨〕
文言論君子全夫智之德則事無不立矣甚矣
智之天下之動也君子知正而固守之則智之
德全矣事豈不依之而立哉文言申乾彖傳之
意及此謂夫天之四德有所謂貞也于人則爲
===
智焉君子何以能全之邪誠以正本於天命之
微知之而能守者寡矣君子則心體虛明于惕
厲之餘於凡正理之渾然者而固守之不移發
于人道之著守之而能固者鮮矣君子則義理
昭融于進修之後於凡正理之燦然者而服膺
之弗失介豫之石不以久暫而或殊所謂利居
貞者有巳秉晉之昭不以順逆而或異所謂大
居正者是巳夫君子之貞固如此吾知中無定
見者事多眩惑也今則以正爲之依據而泛應
punctuated:
易矣。
同考試官教諭潘，批〔易義類能言之，求其粹淨精〕〔微者，無踰此篇。〕
考試官教授吳，批〔非精于易者不能，故錄。〕
考試官教授王，批〔得文言之旨。〕
文言論君子全夫智之德，則事無不立矣。甚矣，智之天下之動也！君子知正而固守之，則智之德全矣，事豈不依之而立哉？文言申乾彖傳之意，及此謂夫天之四德，有所謂貞也，于人則爲智焉。君子何以能全之邪？誠以正本於天命之微，知之而能守者寡矣。君子則心體虛明于惕厲之餘，於凡正理之渾然者，而固守之不移。發于人道之著，守之而能固者鮮矣。君子則義理昭融于進修之後，於凡正理之燦然者，而服膺之弗失。介豫之石，不以久暫而或殊，所謂利居貞者有巳；秉晉之昭，不以順逆而或異，所謂大居正者是巳。夫君子之貞固如此，吾知中無定見者，事多眩惑也。今則以正爲之依據，而泛應
translation_en:
…the Changes.

Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor, comments: 〔Most can expound the meaning of the Changes, but if one seeks purity, refinement, and subtlety,〕〔no essay surpasses this one.〕

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: 〔Only someone deeply versed in the Changes could accomplish this; hence its inclusion.〕

Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: 〔It captures the purport of the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan).〕

The Commentary on the Words of the Text argues that when the gentleman perfects the virtue of wisdom, there is no undertaking he cannot establish. Profound indeed is wisdom’s relation to the movements of the world [?]! When the gentleman knows what is correct and holds firmly to it, the virtue of wisdom is complete. How could his undertakings fail to find support in it and become established? The Commentary on the Words of the Text develops the meaning of the Commentary on the Judgment for Qian. At this point it says that among Heaven’s four virtues is what is called steadfast correctness; in human beings, this is wisdom. How can the gentleman perfect it? Truly, correctness is rooted in the subtle workings of Heaven’s mandate, and few who know it can hold to it. But through vigilance and apprehension, the gentleman renders the substance of his mind clear and receptive, firmly holding without deviation to correct principle in its undivided entirety. Correctness manifests itself in the evident workings of the human way, yet few who hold to it can remain firm. But through advancing in learning and cultivating himself, the gentleman achieves a luminous comprehension of moral principle, cherishing and never losing correct principle in all its brilliant manifestations.

With the rocklike firmness described in Yu, Enthusiasm, he does not vary according to whether the time is long or short: this exemplifies what is called ‘it is beneficial to abide in steadfast correctness’ [?]. Upholding the brightness of Jin, Advance, he does not change with favorable or adverse circumstances: this is what is called ‘the great must abide in correctness.’ Such is the gentleman’s steadfast firmness. I know that those who lack settled discernment within are often bewildered in their undertakings. Now, however, he takes correctness as his foundation and responds to all circumstances…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
有曲當之妙素無定守者事多叢脞也今則以
正爲之憑藉而施爲無凝滯之虞事有是非也
正以立之而卓乎其有本猶長短之依乎度也
事有常變也正以植之而秩乎其有序猶輕重
之依乎權也是豈不足以爲事之幹也哉是何
也天下無正外之理亦無理外之事一正立而
萬事隨之君子體乾之功如是則天德之貞不
在天而在君子矣抑乾之德大矣故易于乾必
以天道聖人明之而此則言君子何也蓋非天
道無以盡乾非聖人無以配乾非君子則亦無
以體乾也君子體乾之德猶夫乾焉則一聖人
一天而已矣周子曰賢希聖聖希天其此之謂
歟然非至健則亦莫之能也已故曰君子以自
疆不息
===
有大者不可以盈故受之以謙有大而能
謙必豫故受之以豫
賀謹　徐
同考試官教諭馬　批　〔序卦題頭緒多端且意對兩〕
punctuated:
有曲當之妙。素無定守者，事多叢脞也；今則以正爲之憑藉，而施爲無凝滯之虞。事有是非也，正以立之，而卓乎其有本，猶長短之依乎度也；事有常變也，正以植之，而秩乎其有序，猶輕重之依乎權也。是豈不足以爲事之幹也哉？是何也？天下無正外之理，亦無理外之事。一正立而萬事隨之。君子體乾之功如是，則天德之貞不在天而在君子矣。抑乾之德大矣，故《易》于乾必以天道、聖人明之，而此則言君子，何也？蓋非天道無以盡乾，非聖人無以配乾，非君子則亦無以體乾也。君子體乾之德，猶夫乾焉，則一聖人、一天而已矣。周子曰：「賢希聖，聖希天。」其此之謂歟？然非至健，則亦莫之能也已。故曰：「君子以自疆不息。」

有大者不可以盈，故受之以謙；有大而能謙，必豫，故受之以豫。

賀謹　徐

同考試官教諭馬，批：〔序卦題，頭緒多端，且意對兩〕
translation_en:
…there is the subtle ability to respond fittingly to every particular circumstance. Those who ordinarily lack a firm commitment are often confused and ineffectual in their affairs; now, taking correctness as their support, they act without fear of obstruction or stagnation. Affairs involve right and wrong: correctness establishes them firmly upon a foundation, just as lengths depend upon a measure. Affairs involve both constant principles and changing circumstances: correctness grounds them in orderly arrangement, just as weights depend upon a balance. Is this not sufficient to serve as the mainstay of affairs? Why is this so? Under Heaven there is no principle outside correctness, nor any affair outside principle. Once correctness is established, the myriad affairs follow it. Such is the achievement of the gentleman in embodying Qian, the Creative: the steadfast correctness of Heaven’s virtue then resides not in Heaven but in the gentleman.

Moreover, the virtue of Qian is great. Thus the Book of Changes invariably explains Qian through the Way of Heaven and the sage. Why, then, does this passage speak of the gentleman? Without the Way of Heaven, Qian cannot be fully expressed; without the sage, Qian cannot be matched; and without the gentleman, Qian cannot be embodied. When the gentleman embodies Qian’s virtue and becomes like Qian itself, he is simply a sage, simply Heaven. Master Zhou said, “The worthy aspires to the sage; the sage aspires to Heaven.” Is this not what he meant? Yet without the utmost vigor, no one can accomplish it. Hence it is said, “The gentleman thereby strengthens himself without ceasing.”

“Those who possess greatness must not become full of themselves; therefore it is followed by Qian, Modesty. Possessing greatness yet being capable of modesty necessarily brings contentment; therefore it is followed by Yu, Contentment.”

He Jin 賀謹; Xu 徐 [?].

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
〔文不偶作者甚難是作備詞發義〕〔昭若不爲所宜錄之〕
同考試官教諭黃　批〔持盈致豫之道分析明白他〕
〔日以此致用必有大過人者高薦允宜〕
同考試官教諭潘　批〔此題甚有關世道子之文足〕
〔以發之殆善於鳴世者〕
考試官教授吳　批〔語不泥而意貫相承善作序〕
〔卦文字者〕
考試官教授王　批〔講不可盈數語讀之令人惕〕
〔然〕
===
存君道之大戒致治道之益隆卦之所以序也
甚矣君道莫患於自盈也戒以從謙而天下之
治有不益隆者哉夫子傳序卦發明大有謙豫
相承之義若曰恒人之見踈每悔禍於無及聖
人之慮遠必防患於未然何則玉帛萬國撫大
統而無虞儲積九年徵太平於有象天下時乎
其大有也有大可樂也亦可憂也人君處此鮮
不因之以自盈者矣君盈而天下之治索矣蓋
好大喜功盈而誇也窮奢極欲盈而侈也流連
punctuated:
〔文不偶，作者甚難。是作備詞發義，〕〔昭若不爲所，宜錄之。〕
同考試官教諭黃批〔持盈致豫之道，分析明白。他〕〔日以此致用，必有大過人者，高薦允宜。〕
同考試官教諭潘批〔此題甚有關世道，子之文足〕〔以發之，殆善於鳴世者。〕
考試官教授吳批〔語不泥而意貫，相承，善作序〕〔卦文字者。〕
考試官教授王批〔講不可盈數語，讀之令人惕〕〔然。〕
存君道之大戒，致治道之益隆，卦之所以序也。甚矣，君道莫患於自盈也！戒以從謙，而天下之治有不益隆者哉？夫子傳《序卦》，發明大有、謙、豫相承之義，若曰：恒人之見踈，每悔禍於無及；聖人之慮遠，必防患於未然。何則？玉帛萬國，撫大統而無虞；儲積九年，徵太平於有象。天下時乎其大有也！有大，可樂也，亦可憂也。人君處此，鮮不因之以自盈者矣。君盈而天下之治索矣。蓋好大喜功，盈而誇也；窮奢極欲，盈而侈也；流連
translation_en:
…the passages are not parallel, making the writer’s task exceedingly difficult. This composition fully develops its wording and brings out the meaning clearly [the phrase 昭若不爲所 is doubtful]. It deserves inclusion.

Associate Examiner Huang, Instructor, comments: “The way to maintain fullness and bring about Contentment is analyzed clearly. If he puts this into practice in the future, he will surely achieve something far surpassing others. A high recommendation is entirely fitting.”

Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor, comments: “This topic bears closely upon the condition of the world, and your essay adequately brings out its significance. You are surely adept at making your voice heard in the world.”

Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The language is not hidebound, and the meaning runs coherently through the successive connections. This is someone skilled at writing essays on the Sequence of the Hexagrams.”

Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: “The few sentences explaining why one must not become self-satisfied inspire apprehensive vigilance in the reader.”

To preserve the great admonition governing the ruler’s way, and to bring the way of good government to still greater flourishing: this is why the hexagrams are arranged in their sequence. How grave it is! In the ruler’s way, nothing is more troubling than self-satisfaction. If he takes warning and follows Modesty, could the governance of All-under-Heaven fail to flourish still further? In his commentary, the Sequence of the Hexagrams, the Master elucidated why Great Possession, Modesty, and Contentment follow one another. It is as though he said: ordinary people’s understanding is deficient, and they often regret calamity only when it is too late; the sage’s deliberations reach far ahead, and he invariably guards against trouble before it arises. Why is this so? The myriad states present jade and silk, and the ruler presides over the great imperial succession without anxiety; stores sufficient for nine years give tangible evidence of great peace. All-under-Heaven is then indeed in a time of Great Possession! Possessing greatness is cause for joy, but also cause for concern. Few rulers in this position fail to become self-satisfied on its account. Once the ruler becomes self-satisfied, the good governance of All-under-Heaven falls into decline. For delighting in grand undertakings and rejoicing in achievements is self-satisfaction expressed as boastfulness; exhausting the possibilities of luxury and indulging desire to the utmost is self-satisfaction expressed as extravagance; lingering in pleasure…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
荒亡怠且危也恃厥有而喪厥有矣如之何其
可哉此大有之後所以必受之以謙也謙者有
而不居之謂也盛滿之戒不於斯而見乎民生
已遂如傷之視方深王道大行不顯之敬愈篤
有大而能謙如此也此君之美也亦民之福也
人君持此未必望之以由豫者然君謙而天下
之和應矣蓋刑清民服豫之昭也作樂崇德豫
之暢也雍熙太和盛以極也感於上而應於下
矣有不可必之理哉此謙卦之後所以必受之
===
以豫也豫者人心和樂以應其上也謙德之終
不於斯而徵乎吁人君不以天下之樂私其身
而天下之民將亦不使吾君終於戚矣相須之
殷有如此哉大抵人君一心關天下之理亂而
敬肆之間存否係之不可不謹也故一少康也
始敗而終成一明宗也先治而後亂何也一臨
難而知懼一既濟而心懈故也周公無逸之作
其萬世君天下之心法乎成王克終保文武於
不墜者公之力也公固深於易者也
punctuated: 荒亡，怠且危也，恃厥有而喪厥有矣，如之何其可哉？此大有之後所以必受之以謙也。謙者，有而不居之謂也。盛滿之戒，不於斯而見乎？民生已遂，如傷之視方深；王道大行，不顯之敬愈篤。有大而能謙如此也，此君之美也，亦民之福也。人君持此，未必望之以由豫者，然君謙而天下之和應矣。蓋刑清民服，豫之昭也；作樂崇德，豫之暢也；雍熙太和，盛以極也。感於上而應於下矣，有不可必之理哉？此謙卦之後所以必受之以豫也。豫者，人心和樂以應其上也。謙德之終，不於斯而徵乎？吁！人君不以天下之樂私其身，而天下之民將亦不使吾君終於戚矣。相須之殷，有如此哉！大抵人君一心關天下之理亂，而敬肆之間，存否係之，不可不謹也。故一少康也，始敗而終成；一明宗也，先治而後亂。何也？一臨難而知懼，一既濟而心懈故也。周公《無逸》之作，其萬世君天下之心法乎？成王克終保文武於不墜者，公之力也。公固深於《易》者也。
translation_en: …abandoning oneself to hunting and drink brings negligence and danger. Relying on what one possesses, one loses those very possessions. How could this be acceptable? This is why Great Possession (Dayou) must be followed by Modesty (Qian). Modesty means possessing without claiming credit. Is not the warning against excessive fullness evident here? Though the people’s livelihood is already secure, the ruler’s concern for them, as though they were injured, only deepens; though the kingly Way prevails widely, his reverence even in the unseen grows more steadfast. Such is possessing greatness while remaining modest. This is an excellence of the ruler and a blessing for the people. A ruler who maintains this disposition need not necessarily expect to become the source of Joy; yet when the ruler is modest, all under Heaven respond in harmony. Clear and equitable punishments and a compliant people manifest Joy; making music to exalt virtue gives Joy full expression; concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony bring flourishing to its height. An influence exerted above evokes a response below. Could there be any reason why this should not assuredly occur? This is why the hexagram Modesty must be followed by Joy (Yu). Joy means that the people’s hearts respond to their sovereign with harmony and gladness. Is not the ultimate effect of the virtue of modesty demonstrated here? Ah! If the ruler does not reserve the joys of the world for his own person, the people of the world will likewise not let their ruler end in sorrow. How profound is their mutual dependence! In general, the ruler’s single heart determines whether all under Heaven enjoys order or suffers disorder; preservation or loss hinges on whether he is reverent or unrestrained. He cannot but exercise care. Thus Shaokang began in defeat but ended in achievement, while Mingzong enjoyed order at first but disorder afterward. Why? Because the one knew fear when confronting adversity, while the other grew lax at heart once success had been attained. Surely the Duke of Zhou’s composition of Against Idleness (Wuyi) provides a method of cultivating the heart for those who rule all under Heaven in every age! That King Cheng could preserve to the end the legacy of Kings Wen and Wu without letting it fall was due to the Duke’s efforts. The Duke indeed possessed a profound understanding of the Book of Changes.

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
書
咨汝羲曁和朞三百有六旬有六日以閏
月定四時成歲允釐百工庶績咸熙
江治
同考試官訓導吴　批〔合天日與月相會之間以置閏而後朞自朞歲自歲明白明有許多道理在塲中士子〕〔類不得其要領故言皆錯雜無章而理反晦此作獨得之當錄出以詔多士〕
同考試官訓導張　批〔曆數難齊亦難言此作說氣朔處明白要是不輕於言者〕
考試官教授吴　批〔文義切當無一浮語足爲經〕
式
===
考試官教授王　批〔隱括傳語成文自然精到〕
聖君總命曆官責以治曆之成功而期以治官
之成效也甚矣天人之相因也術不遠天則政
不失時矣孰謂曆成而治有不成哉想昔帝堯
之意以謂治曆者爲治之先務而置閏者造曆
之全功惟汝羲及和也曷既厥心乎哉何則日
punctuated:
書

「咨！汝羲曁和，朞三百有六旬有六日，以閏月定四時成歲，允釐百工，庶績咸熙。」

江治

同考試官訓導吴批〔合天日與月相會之間以置閏，而後朞自朞，歲自歲。明白明，有許多道理。在塲中士子〕〔類不得其要領，故言皆錯雜無章，而理反晦。此作獨得之，當錄出以詔多士。〕

同考試官訓導張批〔曆數難齊，亦難言。此作說氣朔處明白，要是不輕於言者。〕

考試官教授吴批〔文義切當，無一浮語，足爲經〕式。

考試官教授王批〔隱括傳語成文，自然精到。〕

聖君總命曆官，責以治曆之成功，而期以治官之成效也。甚矣，天人之相因也！術不遠天，則政不失時矣。孰謂曆成而治有不成哉？想昔帝堯之意，以謂治曆者爲治之先務，而置閏者造曆之全功。惟汝羲及和也，曷既厥心乎哉？何則？日…
translation_en:
Book of Documents

“Ah! You, Xi and He: the annual cycle comprises three hundred and sixty-six days. By means of an intercalary month, fix the four seasons and complete the year. Faithfully regulate the hundred offices, and all achievements will flourish.”

Jiang Zhi

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Assistant Instructor: “Combine the intervals at which heaven, the sun, and the moon come together [?] to establish intercalation; only then can the annual cycle and the calendar year each be properly distinguished. The explanation is clear [?], and contains much sound reasoning. Candidates in the examination hall generally fail to grasp the essentials, so their statements are confused and disordered, obscuring the principles instead. This composition alone grasps them; it should be transcribed to instruct the many scholars.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: “Calendrical calculations are difficult to reconcile and also difficult to explain. This composition explains the solar terms and lunar conjunctions clearly. Its author is surely someone who does not make statements lightly.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor: “The composition’s meaning is precise and apt, without a single empty phrase. It deserves to serve as a standard.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: “It recasts the commentary’s wording into a composition that is natural, refined, and thorough.”

The sage ruler issued a comprehensive charge to the calendrical officials, holding them responsible for successfully establishing the calendar and expecting effective administration of the offices to follow. How profound is the interdependence of Heaven and humanity! If calendrical techniques do not depart from Heaven, government will not miss the proper seasons. Who could say that, once the calendar is successfully established, government might fail to be brought into order? I imagine that Emperor Yao’s intention in ancient times was this: establishing the calendar is the first task of government, while instituting intercalation completes the work of making the calendar. You, Xi and He—why would you not devote your minds fully to this? Why is this so? The sun…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
行之繞於地也日惟一周天行之健於日也日
惟一度積天日之贏縮而復於一周之始適氣
運之更始而遂爲一歲之朞焉一朞之中因天
日之差爲三百六十五度而有奇故歲日之數
爲三百六十六日而有定然歲以該月月以該
日則止於三百六十而歲運常舒月朔不足率
餘夫十日有奇故必合所餘之日而置閏積三
歲之餘而爲月使歲氣之有餘者有閏以消其
盈月朔之不足者有閏以益其虛則春夏秋冬
===
之序物候舉不忒其常而時令以正也子丑寅
卯以下辰位皆不易其次而歲功以成也斯可
謂全曆矣由是以之而授人也則令無爽忒而
率作於庶官者有常規政無愆違而責成於百
職者有定守將見政績之統於有位者自農桑
以降非一事也課功覈實之有所程皆及時而
惠叙矣治功之蒞於在官者凡民事所關非一
端也月要歲會之有其度皆順時而均次矣功
豈有不廣治豈有不成哉吁治道因於時而非
punctuated: 行之繞於地也，日惟一周；天行之健於日也，日惟一度。積天日之贏縮，而復於一周之始，適氣運之更始，而遂爲一歲之朞焉。一朞之中，因天日之差，爲三百六十五度而有奇，故歲日之數爲三百六十六日而有定。然歲以該月，月以該日，則止於三百六十，而歲運常舒，月朔不足，率餘夫十日有奇。故必合所餘之日而置閏，積三歲之餘而爲月，使歲氣之有餘者有閏以消其盈，月朔之不足者有閏以益其虛，則春夏秋冬之序，物候舉不忒其常，而時令以正也；子丑寅卯以下辰位，皆不易其次，而歲功以成也。斯可謂全曆矣！由是以之而授人也，則令無爽忒，而率作於庶官者有常規；政無愆違，而責成於百職者有定守。將見政績之統於有位者，自農桑以降，非一事也，課功覈實之有所程，皆及時而惠叙矣；治功之蒞於在官者，凡民事所關，非一端也，月要歲會之有其度，皆順時而均次矣。功豈有不廣，治豈有不成哉？吁！治道因於時，而非
translation_en:
…its course circles the earth, making just one circuit each day; Heaven’s movement outpaces the sun by just one degree each day. As the gains and losses between Heaven and the sun accumulate, they return to the beginning of a circuit, coinciding with the renewal of the cycle of seasonal qi and thus completing a year. Within one annual cycle, the difference between Heaven and the sun amounts to three hundred and sixty-five degrees and a fraction; hence the number of days in a year is fixed at three hundred and sixty-six. Yet when the year is reckoned by its months and the months by their days, the total is only three hundred and sixty. The annual cycle thus consistently extends beyond this, while the lunar months fall short, leaving an excess of ten days and a fraction on average. It is therefore necessary to combine the remaining days and insert an intercalary month, accumulating the surplus of three years to make a month. Intercalation absorbs the excess in the annual cycle of seasonal qi and supplies the deficiency in the lunar months. Thus, in the succession of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, the signs of the seasons all retain their regular patterns, and seasonal ordinances are correctly timed. The positions designated zi, chou, yin, mao, and the subsequent earthly branches all retain their proper sequence, and the work of the year is accomplished. This may be called a complete calendar!

When this is used to communicate the seasons to the people, commands will contain no errors, and there will be constant rules for directing the work of the various officials; government measures will involve no departures from what is proper, and there will be fixed duties for holding the many offices responsible for results. We shall then see that the administrative achievements overseen by those in positions of authority—from agriculture and sericulture onward—encompass more than a single undertaking. With established standards for assessing achievements and verifying actual results, all will be carried out in season and harmoniously ordered. The work of government administered by officeholders likewise embraces many aspects of the people’s affairs. With proper measures for monthly summaries and annual accounts, all will follow the seasons and be equitably arranged. How could achievements fail to expand, or good government fail to be realized? Ah! The way of governing depends upon the seasons, and without …

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
曆不明人時叙於曆而非閏不備聖人立法如
此其敬天勤民之意至矣抑考之叙堯典者首
以授時叙舜典者首以齊政蓋王者履端於始
故審時爲先歸餘於終故置閏爲備亦可見當
時君臣莫非通達天人貫徹三才者也後世俗
儒無事於曆而治曆者非儒何望其能明哉自
夏氏以來而羲和合爲一後世殆無專官矣何
望其能明哉
寛而有制從容以和
周宗正
同考試官訓導吳　批　〔聖人所謂寛和者寛中自有制和中自有從容作者多以有制濟寛從容濟和殆失之〕
〔矣此作得之宜録出以爲經學式〕
同考試官訓導張　批　〔成王命君陳繼周公謀數之後正欲其以寛和致治之意也此作發揮殆盡〕
考試官教授吳　批　〔文字有筆力可取〕
考試官教授王　批　〔讀是篇可以見忠厚立國意〕
punctuated:
曆不明，人時叙於曆而非閏不備。聖人立法如此，其敬天勤民之意至矣！抑考之，叙《堯典》者首以授時，叙《舜典》者首以齊政。蓋王者履端於始，故審時爲先；歸餘於終，故置閏爲備。亦可見當時君臣莫非通達天人、貫徹三才者也。後世俗儒無事於曆，而治曆者非儒，何望其能明哉？自夏氏以來，而羲和合爲一，後世殆無專官矣，何望其能明哉？

寛而有制，從容以和。
周宗正

同考試官訓導吳批：〔聖人所謂寛和者，寛中自有制，和中自有從容。作者多以有制濟寛，從容濟和，殆失之〕〔矣。此作得之，宜録出以爲經學式。〕
同考試官訓導張批：〔成王命君陳繼周公謀數之後，正欲其以寛和致治之意也。此作發揮殆盡。〕
考試官教授吳批：〔文字有筆力，可取。〕
考試官教授王批：〔讀是篇，可以見忠厚立國意。〕
translation_en:
… cannot be made clear without a calendar; the seasons for human activities are ordered through the calendar, but without intercalation it is incomplete. Such were the institutions established by the sages: their intention to revere Heaven and attend diligently to the people was consummate! Moreover, examining the matter, the account in the Canon of Yao begins with granting the seasons, while that in the Canon of Shun begins with regulating celestial movements. A true king establishes the starting point at the beginning, and therefore gives priority to determining the seasons; he gathers the remainder at the end, and therefore inserts an intercalary month to complete the system. This also shows that the rulers and ministers of that time all understood Heaven and humanity and thoroughly comprehended the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. In later ages, commonplace Confucian scholars had no involvement with calendrical matters, while those who worked on the calendar were not Confucian scholars. How could one expect them to understand it clearly? Since the Xia dynasty, the offices of Xi and He have been combined into one; in later ages there have scarcely been officials specifically charged with these duties. How could one expect them to understand it clearly?

“Be generous yet measured, composed and harmonious.”
By Zhou Zongzheng.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Assistant Instructor: “What the sages call generosity and harmony means that generosity itself contains measure, and harmony itself contains composure. Most writers take measure as a corrective to generosity and composure as a corrective to harmony, thereby missing the point. This composition grasps it correctly and should be copied out as a model for classical scholarship.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: “When King Cheng commanded Jun Chen to succeed to the Duke of Zhou’s plans and arrangements [?], his precise intention was that Jun Chen should achieve good government through generosity and harmony. This composition develops that meaning almost exhaustively.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Instructor: “The writing has force and merits acceptance.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Instructor: “Reading this essay, one can discern the intention to establish the state upon loyalty and generosity.”

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
而從容乎道德之漸磨游息化養而厭飫乎禮
義之涵育弗若汝政者化誘之自如也弗化汝
訓者陶鎔之常在也譬若春風之長養而披拂
之力寓焉和以處民如此吾見夫在繼世也猶
夫在先王也又何有自作不典而撓治者哉吁
寬可能也寬而有制未易能也和可能也和而
從容未易能也達權濟變以成和中之治不有
望於汝君陳也耶嗟夫愚於是知周之所以處
殷民者至矣初命周公以師保之尊謹毖之繼
命君陳以寬和委曲化導之似亦未見其盡帖
然者至康王之時既歷三紀復命畢公以成終
之責保釐之然後世已變而風始移也嗚呼觀
其化之難可以見殷之先王及民之德觀其
頑獷之性卒變爲良民又可以見周之先王化
民之仁
詩
鴥彼飛隼其飛戾天亦集爰止方叔涖止
其車三千師干之試方叔率止鉦人伐
punctuated:
而從容乎道德之漸磨，游息化養，而厭飫乎禮義之涵育。弗若汝政者，化誘之自如也；弗化汝訓者，陶鎔之常在也。譬若春風之長養，而披拂之力寓焉。和以處民如此，吾見夫在繼世也，猶夫在先王也，又何有自作不典而撓治者哉？吁！寬可能也，寬而有制未易能也；和可能也，和而從容未易能也。達權濟變，以成和中之治，不有望於汝君陳也耶？嗟夫！愚於是知周之所以處殷民者至矣。初命周公以師保之尊謹毖之，繼命君陳以寬和委曲化導之，似亦未見其盡帖然者。至康王之時，既歷三紀，復命畢公以成終之責保釐之，然後世已變而風始移也。嗚呼！觀其化之難，可以見殷之先王及民之德；觀其頑獷之性卒變爲良民，又可以見周之先王化民之仁。

詩

鴥彼飛隼，其飛戾天，亦集爰止。方叔涖止，其車三千，師干之試。方叔率止，鉦人伐
translation_en:
…and, at ease amid the gradual polishing of the Way and virtue, they roam and rest under its transforming nurture, becoming fully steeped in the sustaining influence of ritual and righteousness. Those who do not conform to your government are transformed and guided with ease; for those who are not transformed by your instruction, the work of molding and refining remains constant. It is like the nurturing spring wind, within which resides the power to stir and move things. When the people are treated with such harmony, I see that under the succeeding ruler things remain as they were under the former king. How, then, could anyone devise irregular practices of his own and disrupt good government? Ah! Leniency may be possible, but leniency with restraint is not easily achieved. Harmony may be possible, but harmony maintained with unhurried ease is not easily achieved. To understand expedient measures and meet changing circumstances, thereby achieving harmonious and balanced government—is this not what is expected of you, Jun Chen?

Alas! From this I, in my ignorance, understand how consummate were Zhou’s methods of dealing with the people of Yin. First, the Duke of Zhou was commissioned, with the dignity of a preceptor and protector, to watch over them cautiously. Next, Jun Chen was commissioned to transform and guide them with leniency and harmony, accommodating their circumstances in every particular. Yet it seems that they were still not entirely compliant. By the time of King Kang, three twelve-year cycles had elapsed. The Duke of Bi was then commissioned to safeguard and govern them, charged with bringing the undertaking to completion. Only then, after a generation had passed, did their customs begin to change. Ah! In the difficulty of transforming them, we can see how deeply the virtue of Yin’s former kings had reached the people. In the eventual transformation of their stubborn and unruly dispositions into those of good subjects, we can also see the benevolence with which Zhou’s former kings transformed the people.

Book of Odes

Swift is that flying falcon; its flight reaches heaven, yet it also alights and rests here. Fang Shu has arrived, with three thousand chariots, his host and shields arrayed [?]. Fang Shu leads them; the gong officers strike…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
鼓陳師鞠旅顯允方叔伐鼓淵淵振旅
闐闐
胡文宗
同考試官教諭許　批〔前後興詞俱在六句止而此與尤有意作者往往以衆盛有節對言且於進退之處截〕
〔於經文䟽漏殊甚此作精練以昌其詞紆廻以發其趣知非風騷篇章所能限也〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔師盛有節正見古人用兵多〕
〔多蓋善處此作曲盡其意可錄〕
考試官教授吳　批〔文字嚴整且有步驟佳士佳〕
〔士〕
考試官教授王　批〔爲文亦有紀律〕
===
詩人興大將之師盛而有節而遂詳其實也蓋
行師之要以律爲臧也方叔爲將而進退有節
如此此其所以不戰而屈人之兵與釆芑之詩
宣王命方叔南征而軍士作此謂夫載瞻鴥彼
之飛隼也上焉傅于天下焉翔而集勢不終于
飛也而有時乎止矣况我方叔之涖止也其車
punctuated:
鼓，陳師鞠旅。顯允方叔，伐鼓淵淵，振旅闐闐。
胡文宗。
同考試官教諭許，批〔前後興詞俱在六句止，而此與尤有意。作者往往以衆盛有節對言，且於進退之處截〕〔於經文䟽漏殊甚。此作精練以昌其詞，紆廻以發其趣，知非風騷篇章所能限也。〕
同考試官教諭朱，批〔師盛有節，正見古人用兵多〕〔多蓋善處。此作曲盡其意，可錄。〕
考試官教授吳，批〔文字嚴整，且有步驟。佳士，佳〕〔士！〕
考試官教授王，批〔爲文亦有紀律。〕

translation_en:
…the drums; they array the troops and muster the host. Illustrious and trustworthy is Fang Shu: the drums resound deeply, and the troops withdraw with a swelling din.
By Hu Wenzong.
Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “The evocative passages before and after both end at the sixth line, and this evocation is especially meaningful [?]. Writers often discuss the army’s multitude and its discipline as paired themes, and break off at the passages concerning advance and withdrawal, thereby leaving serious gaps in their treatment of the canonical text. This composition gives its language fullness through refinement and develops its meaning through winding elaboration. Clearly, it cannot be confined within the bounds of the Airs and the Songs of Chu.”
Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “The army’s strength in numbers and its discipline precisely reveal how the ancients employed troops: the more numerous, the better they handled them [?]. This composition fully develops the subtleties of that meaning and merits inclusion.”
Examiner Wu, Professor, comments: “The writing is rigorous and well ordered, and proceeds in measured stages. An excellent scholar, an excellent scholar!”
Examiner Wang, Professor, comments: “His composition, too, observes military discipline.”
The poet evocatively introduces the great commander’s army as numerous yet disciplined, and then sets forth the particulars. For the essential virtue in conducting an army lies in discipline. As commander, Fang Shu maintained such order in advance and withdrawal: was this not how he subdued another’s forces without fighting? The poem ‘Gathering Millet’ (Cai qi) was composed by the soldiers when King Xuan ordered Fang Shu to campaign in the south. Its meaning is this: look at that swiftly flying falcon. Above, it reaches the sky; below, it wheels and alights. Its movement does not consist solely in flight: there are times when it rests. How much more so when our Fang Shu arrives! His chariots…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
有三千之衆師干有練習之美法不一于進也
而有時乎退焉故即其將戰而觀之我方叔之
率止也以爲兵雖多矣無制者敗于爲鉦人伐
鉦所以肅其選徒之警也鼓人伐鼓所以先其
赴敵之聲也既動闐之又靜翕之而如山如川
之勢其在於斯乎兵雖練矣不令奚從于焉既
陳我師而昭其用命之誓復陳我旅而肅以止
齊之規既三令之又五申之而攻城攻心之道
其出於是乎是則其將戰之有節也固如此又
===
即其始終而觀之彼顯允之方叔也以爲兵出
而無以治之則亂由是伐鼓淵淵使凡聞是聲
者勇者不必先而怯者不敢後同此行枚同此
聲討其視治兵也一視其將戰也旅入而無以
振之則散由是伐鼓闐闐使凡得於耳者前軍
無敢過後軍無不及以是結陳以是凱還其視
振旅也一視其治兵也是則其始終之有節也
又如此吁此方叔之兵所以先爲不可勝而蠻
荆之服正所以破其心與抑論之語曰君不擇
punctuated: 有三千之衆，師干有練習之美，法不一于進也，而有時乎退焉。故即其將戰而觀之，我方叔之率止也，以爲兵雖多矣，無制者敗。于爲鉦人伐鉦，所以肅其選徒之警也；鼓人伐鼓，所以先其赴敵之聲也。既動闐之，又靜翕之，而如山如川之勢，其在於斯乎？兵雖練矣，不令奚從？于焉既陳我師，而昭其用命之誓；復陳我旅，而肅以止齊之規。既三令之，又五申之，而攻城攻心之道，其出於是乎？是則其將戰之有節也，固如此。又即其始終而觀之，彼顯允之方叔也，以爲兵出而無以治之則亂。由是伐鼓淵淵，使凡聞是聲者，勇者不必先，而怯者不敢後，同此行枚，同此聲討。其視治兵也，一視其將戰也。旅入而無以振之則散。由是伐鼓闐闐，使凡得於耳者，前軍無敢過，後軍無不及，以是結陳，以是凱還。其視振旅也，一視其治兵也。是則其始終之有節也，又如此。吁！此方叔之兵所以先爲不可勝，而蠻荆之服，正所以破其心與？抑論之，語曰：「君不擇」
translation_en:
…numbered three thousand, and his troops possessed the excellence of thorough training. His methods were not confined to advancing: there were also occasions for retreat. Thus, consider him as he was about to engage in battle. In leading his men, our Fang Shu held that, however numerous the troops, those without discipline would be defeated. Accordingly [?], the gong players struck their gongs to make the signals for mustering the men solemn and compelling; the drummers beat their drums to sound the advance against the enemy. He set them moving with a thunderous sound, then brought them together in stillness. Was this not the source of their power, like a mountain or a river? However well trained the troops, without commands, what could they follow? He therefore arrayed our army and made clear the oath to obey orders; he again arrayed our troops and imposed strict rules for halting and keeping ranks aligned. He issued orders three times and reiterated them five times. Did not the means of attacking cities and breaking the enemy’s resolve arise from this? Such, indeed, was his discipline when about to fight.

Consider also his conduct from beginning to end. That illustrious and trustworthy Fang Shu held that troops going forth without proper ordering would fall into disorder. He therefore beat the drums with a deep, resounding sound, so that among all who heard them, the brave would not insist on going ahead, and the timid would not dare fall behind. Together they marched with silence-gags in their mouths; together they proclaimed the enemy’s offenses. He regarded ordering the troops just as he regarded preparing to engage in battle. If troops returning were not marshaled, they would disperse. He therefore beat the drums with a thunderous sound, so that among all who heard them, none in the vanguard dared go too far, and none in the rear failed to keep up. In this manner they formed ranks; in this manner they returned in triumph. He regarded marshaling the returning troops just as he regarded ordering them when setting forth. Such, too, was his discipline from beginning to end. Ah! This was how Fang Shu’s troops first made themselves invincible; was not the submission of the Man and Jing peoples precisely the result of breaking their resolve? To discuss it further, a saying runs: “The ruler does not choose…”

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教授王　批〔莊重典雅〕
詩人言後王繼先之效天與而人歸之也蓋天
福之所在人心之所在也後王以繼先而得之
前王裕後之休大矣哉詩人美武王能纘太王
王季文王之緒而有天下此則言其裕後之福
謂夫於皇武王達孝繼述乎先後餘休啓佑於
後昆來世而能纘承之則所以仰賴之者何旣
邪是故世德之作求武王之孝通于神明者也
後世能襲之以爲守成之地則仰焉不愧於天
===
矣吾知天命雖難忱也感明德之惟馨隆休祥
以昭其行監宗子之惟肖覃福澤以厚其生安
富尊榮享之而未艾身之所履上帝其默相之
也祿位名壽保之於無窮事之所施鬼神其陰
隲之也以百行之原而�office皇天之福所以保佑
之者依然臨汝之成命矣天之與之後何減於
前耶天命旣集人心焉之于京之克配武王之
孝光于四海者也後王能紹之以爲嗣統之規
則俯焉不怍於人矣吾知人心雖無常也覩君
punctuated:
考試官教授王，批〔莊重典雅〕。

詩人言後王繼先之效，天與而人歸之也。蓋天福之所在，人心之所在也。後王以繼先而得之，前王裕後之休大矣哉！詩人美武王能纘太王、王季、文王之緒而有天下，此則言其裕後之福。謂夫於皇武王，達孝繼述乎先，後餘休啓佑於後昆。來世而能纘承之，則所以仰賴之者何旣邪？是故世德之作求，武王之孝通于神明者也。後世能襲之以爲守成之地，則仰焉不愧於天矣。吾知天命雖難忱也，感明德之惟馨，隆休祥以昭其行；監宗子之惟肖，覃福澤以厚其生。安富尊榮，享之而未艾，身之所履，上帝其默相之也；祿位名壽，保之於無窮，事之所施，鬼神其陰隲之也。以百行之原而�office皇天之福，所以保佑之者，依然臨汝之成命矣。天之與之，後何減於前耶？天命旣集，人心焉之？于京之克配，武王之孝光于四海者也。後王能紹之以爲嗣統之規，則俯焉不怍於人矣。吾知人心雖無常也，覩君
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, Prefectural School Instructor. Comment: 〔Grave and classically elegant.〕

The poet speaks of the results when later kings continue the work of their predecessors: Heaven supports them, and the people turn to them in allegiance. For where Heaven’s blessings rest, there too the people’s hearts incline. Later kings obtain these by continuing their predecessors’ work. How great, then, is the beneficence of former kings in providing for their successors! The poet praises King Wu for continuing the legacy of King Tai, Wang Ji, and King Wen and thereby possessing all under Heaven. Here, however, he speaks of the blessings King Wu secured for his successors. The meaning is that glorious King Wu carried filial piety to its fullest extent by continuing and fulfilling his predecessors’ work, leaving abundant beneficence to guide and protect his descendants. If subsequent generations can carry on this legacy, how could their reliance upon it ever be exhausted [?]? Thus, his seeking to perpetuate the virtue of successive generations was the means by which King Wu’s filial piety reached the spirits. If later generations can inherit it as the foundation for preserving what has been achieved, they can look upward without shame before Heaven.

I know that although Heaven’s mandate is difficult to rely upon, Heaven is moved by the fragrance of illustrious virtue and increases auspicious blessings to make such conduct manifest. It observes that the heir to the ancestral line truly resembles his forebears and spreads blessings to enrich his life. Peace, wealth, honor, and glory are enjoyed without end: wherever he treads, the Lord on High silently assists him. Emolument, rank, reputation, and longevity are preserved without limit: whatever undertakings he carries out, the spirits secretly sustain him. Through the source of all virtuous conduct, he [garbled text: �office] august Heaven’s blessings. What protects and supports him remains the established mandate watching over him. How could Heaven’s support for later generations be any less than its support for earlier ones?

Once Heaven’s mandate has gathered upon him, where will the people’s hearts turn? His being worthy to match his predecessors in the capital was the means by which King Wu’s filial piety shone throughout the Four Seas. If later kings can continue it as their rule for succeeding to the sovereign line, they can look downward without shame before the people. I know that although the people’s hearts are inconstant, when they behold their ruler…

title: 嘉靖四年江西鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導蔡　批〔正時重信皆變周制處作者　〕
〔多所牽合此篇精切明暢是用錄出〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔說法天道正人心處道理甚〕
大
考試官教授吳　批〔發春秋盡易之　意明盡〕
考試官教授王　批〔得聖人變周制之意〕
春秋變周制以從易者所以正時者有所以重
信者此見行夏時善者命聖人無非用權以變
周制也其垂訓之旨深哉丑仲冬周之正朔也
===
經於正月而書春然則正以仲冬冬者非耶蓋時
以作事而殷之建丑周之建子皆非所以授民
時也孰有時之正令之善如夏之建寅者乎建
諸天地質諸鬼神誠歷百王而無弊也春秋酌
先王之禮立萬世之法以治曆明時爲務於此
有得焉若曰月可周也事可魯也時不可以不
行乎夏也雖變周之制何惑焉故於隱之正月
特書春王以冠之殆與殷輅之乘韶舞之用同
一垂法後世之意也此義行則四時以定乜歲
punctuated:
同考試官訓導蔡　批〔正時重信皆變周制處，作者〕〔多所牽合，此篇精切明暢，是用錄出。〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔說法天道、正人心處，道理甚〕大。
考試官教授吳　批〔發春秋盡易之意，明盡。〕
